VCTE, while well validated, has important context‐specific limitations that are particularly relevant to MASLD screening populations. Many individuals targeted for screening are severely obese or have coexisting cardiometabolic disease. In obesity, VCTE is associated with higher rates of technical failure and unreliable measurements, even if the XL probe is used. , In addition, liver stiffness can be falsely elevated in the setting of hepatic congestion, such as in patients with heart failure, leading to overestimation of fibrosis if clinical context is not carefully considered. In contrast, ELF offers a less operator‐dependent, practical, blood‐based alternative with good accuracy and particular utility when imaging capacity is limited or unreliable. A major challenge with ELF relates to threshold selection, which varies across guidelines and clinical contexts and has evolved over time (Table ). Commonly cited cutoffs include ELF <7.7 to rule out advanced fibrosis, ≥9.2 to indicate a high likelihood of clinically significant fibrosis, ≥9.8 to indicate a high likelihood of advanced fibrosis, and ≥11.3 to identify individuals at particularly high risk of cirrhosis or liver‐related events. Of note, ELF is FDA approved for its prognostic value and technically not as a diagnostic tool for liver fibrosis. This variability contributes to the perception that ELF cutoffs represent a ‘moving target’, potentially limiting clinician confidence and uniform adoption. Taken together, existing evidence supports the use of either VCTE or ELF as confirmatory tests, and even other modalities, such as shear wave elastography or MRE, with selection guided by local resources, experience, patient characteristics, and clinical setting, rather than by a clear superiority of one modality over the other. Indeed, as NITs are now used to diagnose MASH with F2–F3 to guide treatment decisions, some of the guidelines recommend using more than one NIT in certain cases to confirm the diagnosis. , While most guidelines , , , focused primarily on fibrosis detection and referral, recent AASLD practice guidance updates , and other expert consensus , provide explicit NIT thresholds to guide initiation and monitoring of resmetirom and semaglutide treatment, without requiring universal liver biopsy. As can be observed in Figure , there is partial agreement between these recommendations, with only small discrepancies, usually related to the ranges where confirmation with an additional NIT is recommended. An important limitation of these ranges is that many of these thresholds are derived from analysing baseline characteristics of the populations which have participated in the randomised controlled trials. In these trials, patients were highly selected, as multiple layers of screening were required in order to enrich for individuals with histologic F2–F3 disease and to minimise unnecessary liver biopsies. Depending on what criteria were used in each trial, the distribution of baseline NIT values will be significantly different, and it does not reflect the spectrum of disease seen in routine clinical practice. Because the observed NIT ranges are conditioned on prior screening and biopsy‐selection criteria, they do not represent unbiased thresholds for identifying treatment‐eligible patients in real‐world populations. Moreover, if we compare the thresholds used to initiate treatment for MASH with F2–F3 (Figure ) with the thresholds used to decide on hepatology referral in prior guidelines, we can observe marked differences, especially for ELF. , , Future guideline frameworks will need to explicitly separate screening efficiency from treatment eligibility and incorporate population‐level validation and outcome‐based calibration of NIT thresholds. But until then, when faced with patients with borderline or discordant NIT values, clinicians will necessarily require individualised clinical judgement. Clinicians will have to decide whether to favour treatment initiation, confirmation with additional NITs, or active surveillance, taking into account the overall cardiometabolic risk profile, comorbidities, and therapeutic risk–benefit balance. From a pragmatic standpoint, when consideration is being given to GLP‐1RAs, it may be reasonable to err towards treatment initiation, given their extensive long‐term safety data, consistent weight loss efficacy, and well‐established cardiovascular and renal benefits, as well as their use across the spectrum of liver disease, including compensated cirrhosis. In contrast, when resmetirom is under consideration, the absence of long‐term outcome data and limited experience in patients with cirrhosis support a more conservative approach, in which confirmation with an additional NIT or short‐interval reassessment may be appropriate before treatment initiation. This differentiated strategy may help clinicians navigate uncertainty at borderline thresholds while minimising both undertreatment and unnecessary exposure to therapies with narrower evidence bases. 9 WHEN TO RULE OUT OTHER LIVER DISEASES AND WHO IS RESPONSIBLE FOR THIS? Across major MASLD guidelines and consensus documents, there is broad agreement that alternative causes of liver disease should be excluded, but the specificity, timing, and ownership of this evaluation are inconsistently defined, , , , , with the exception of the latest AGA MASH Clinical Care Pathway. Most documents explicitly state that other liver diseases should be considered in the differential diagnosis. However, few provide a test‐by‐test checklist of what needs to be ordered, and they are also largely silent on when in the diagnostic pathway this evaluation should occur. This creates ambiguity as to whether comprehensive etiologic testing should precede NIT‐based risk assessment, occur in parallel, or be deferred until abnormal or discordant results prompt referral. Finally, none of the guidelines clearly delineate who is responsible for ruling out alternative liver diseases at each stage of care. While primary care providers, endocrinologists, and obesity specialists are increasingly positioned as the entry point for MASLD screening, the guidelines do not specify which elements of the etiologic work‐up are expected to occur before hepatology referral. In practice, this often leads to variability, with some clinicians ordering extensive panels upfront (sometimes with significant over‐testing) and others deferring nearly all etiologic testing to hepatology referral. In turn, this lack of clarity can also lead to over‐assumption of MASLD as the diagnosis, with the possibility of missing alternative diagnoses, which oftentimes coexist with MASLD. Together, these gaps highlight an important opportunity for future guidelines to more clearly define what to test for and when to test, while offering adaptable guidance on the role of non‐hepatologists in excluding other etiologies of liver fibrosis, recognising that responsibilities will necessarily vary across healthcare settings and reimbursement environments. The 2026 update of the MASH Clinical Care Pathway tried to overcome some of these limitations, by providing explicit guidance on these issues, including tools to screen for alcohol consumption (AUDIT‐C or the National Institutes of Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism [NIAAA] recommended single alcohol screening question), as well as detailed work‐up needed to exclude other liver conditions. An AUDIT‐C score ≥4 (men) or ≥3 (women) indicates a positive screen. Similarly, a response of “≥1” on the NIAAA single alcohol screening question also warrants follow‐up. Following a positive screen, additional questions should be asked to learn the typical weekly pattern and quantify alcohol intake. None of the guidelines devotes much consideration to serum markers of alcohol consumption (e.g., phosphatidyl ethanol [Peth]) despite its increased use in clinical practice, and this option was only mentioned in the newest guidance/consensus. , 10 MANAGEMENT OF INDIVIDUALS WITH <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">MASH</styled-content> WITH <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">F2</styled-content> AND <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">F3</styled-content> The management of MASLD and MASH is undergoing a period of unusually rapid evolution, driven by the emergence of effective pharmacologic therapies, expanding evidence for cardiometabolic interventions, and increasing reliance on NITs to guide treatment decisions. As a result, clinical guidelines are increasingly challenged to balance durability with relevance, and recommendations may become outdated within a short time frame as new trial data, regulatory approvals, and real‐world experience accumulate. This dynamic environment partly explains the heterogeneity observed across contemporary guidelines, which often reflect different evidentiary cutoffs, regulatory contexts, and intended audiences. In this section, we compare areas of broad consensus and key points of divergence across guidelines with respect to lifestyle interventions, bariatric surgery, diabetes management, and MASH‐directed therapies, highlighting where recommendations are robust and where future updates are likely to be required. 10.1 Lifestyle interventions and bariatric surgery Across guidelines, lifestyle modification remains the cornerstone of MASLD/MASH management, yet recommendations are largely superficial. While various dietary approaches are endorsed (e.g., Mediterranean‐style diets, low‐carbohydrate diets, caloric restriction), no guideline recommends one specific dietary pattern over another based on head‐to‐head comparative evidence. This reflects the absence of adequately powered trials directly comparing dietary strategies with histological or fibrosis‐related endpoints in MASLD/MASH. Consequently, recommendations emphasising one diet over another may be premature, and most guidelines appropriately focus on caloric reduction, sustainability, and patient preference rather than diet composition per se. In contrast, weight‐loss targets are remarkably consistent, with most documents converging on ≥5% weight loss for steatosis improvement, ≥7% for histologic benefits, and ≥10% for fibrosis regression. Because lifestyle interventions usually target the shared upstream drivers (i.e., insulin resistance, increased adiposity, and overall cardiometabolic risk), most lifestyle recommendations in MASLD/MASH guidelines are essentially the same as for individuals with obesity and T2D (e.g., caloric restriction, sustained weight loss, macronutrient composition, increased physical activity). Probably, the most ‘liver‐specific’ lifestyle recommendations are alcohol avoidance (particularly once fibrosis is clinically significant) and coffee consumption (e.g., ~3 cups/day in the absence of contraindications), which is not a standard recommendation for obesity or diabetes care despite potentially beneficial for MASLD in epidemiologic data. Most other lifestyle advice in MASLD/MASH, such as limiting sugar‐sweetened beverages/refined carbohydrates, prioritising unsaturated fats/fibre, and structured physical activity, would generally be considered appropriate and beneficial irrespective of liver disease. An in‐depth summary of lifestyle interventions and their evidence in MASLD/MASH is beyond the scope of this review, and readers are referred to several comprehensive reviews that detail the evidence supporting dietary modification, physical activity, and weight loss strategies, as well as their limitations and implementation challenges. , , All major guidelines , , , , , are largely concordant in their recommendations regarding bariatric (or metabolic) surgery in MASLD/MASH. They usually state that bariatric surgery may be considered in patients who meet standard surgical indications based on BMI and obesity‐related comorbidities, and substantial evidence demonstrates improvements in steatosis, inflammation, and fibrosis following surgery. However, MASH itself is not considered a primary indication for bariatric surgery, and surgery should not be pursued solely for the treatment of liver disease in the absence of established metabolic indications. , , , , , Rather, the hepatic benefits are viewed as an important secondary advantage of a procedure undertaken for obesity and its systemic complications. Guidelines further acknowledge that bariatric surgery may be performed safely in carefully selected individuals with compensated cirrhosis, provided that clinically significant portal hypertension is excluded and surgery is undertaken in experienced centres with multidisciplinary expertise. A recent retrospective observational study in individuals with MASH‐related compensated cirrhosis ( n = 168) reported that bariatric surgery was associated with an 80% lower risk of progression to decompensation and a 72% lower risk of incident major liver‐related outcomes. Finally, except for the 2026 AGA MASH Clinical Care Pathway, current MASLD/MASH guidelines do not specifically address the recognised risk of incident alcohol misuse/AUD after bariatric procedures, which can particularly affect individuals with liver disease. Alcohol use should be systematically evaluated before bariatric surgery and reassessed during postoperative follow‐up, with referral to addiction medicine specialists when appropriate. 10.2 Pharmacological management of diabetes in <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">MASH</styled-content> and <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">MASH</styled-content>‐directed therapies As discussed above, the therapeutic landscape of MASH is evolving at an unprecedented pace, highlighting a fundamental gap between the speed at which new evidence emerges and the timeline of guideline development. Indeed, with the exception of the AGA 2026 Updated MASH Clinical Care Pathway, none of the major guidelines were published after the regulatory approval of both semaglutide and resmetirom. Consequently, existing documents provide limited guidance on practical questions such as which agent should be initiated first in patients with MASH and F2–F3 fibrosis. , , , , This gap is not unexpected, but it underscores how quickly guidance can become outdated when new pharmacologic options enter clinical practice. Despite being grounded in evidence‐based medicine, guideline recommendations are inevitably shaped by differences in interpretation of trial data, weighting of endpoints, clinical priorities, and even personal or disciplinary perspectives of the authors. These differences become particularly apparent when evaluating therapies with heterogeneous trial designs, populations, durations, and primary outcomes. Even when acknowledging the metabolic advantages of GLP‐1RA, the most recent AGA 2026 Updated MASH Clinical Care Pathway refrains from recommending a fixed sequence for initiating FDA‐approved MASH therapies. Instead, it emphasises shared decision‐making, implicitly recognising that clinical context, comorbidities, access, and patient preferences may outweigh any single hierarchy of drugs. This approach contrasts with the expectations of many clinicians, who often turn to guidelines specifically for help in making such prioritisation decisions. While a flexible framework may be philosophically defensible, it may also reduce the practical utility of guidelines for front‐line decision‐making. A similar pattern is seen in the approach followed by AASLD, , where independent updates for semaglutide and resmetirom are provided, yet no formal guidance is offered on how to choose between them. Notably, although guidelines consistently emphasise the importance of a holistic (multidisciplinary) approach to MASH, accounting for cardiovascular disease, chronic kidney disease, heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, obstructive sleep apnea, and other obesity‐related complications, these comorbidities are not always explicitly integrated into therapeutic prioritisation. This omission is particularly striking given that GLP‐1RA (or dual agonists) have demonstrated benefits across many of these conditions. , , , From a pragmatic standpoint, it is difficult to argue against the use of GLP‐1–based therapy as first‐line treatment in patients with MASH who also have overweight, obesity, and/or type 2 diabetes, if no contraindications exist. In this context, the question becomes less whether a GLP‐1RA should be used, and more which agent should be selected. And this is another question that is amenable to subjectivity. Although fibrosis improvement was not the primary endpoint of the phase 2 trial of tirzepatide in MASH, the magnitude of histologic improvement observed in this randomised, controlled trial has led several authors to view this as convincing evidence of antifibrotic benefit, warranting similar clinical consideration as semaglutide, as observed in the framework for the pharmacological treatment of obesity from the EASO or the AACE Consensus Statement on Obesity treatment from 2025. Others may reasonably argue that tirzepatide must demonstrate comparable effects in a larger phase 3 trial before being positioned equivalently. This divergence highlights an important conceptual distinction between regulatory requirements for approval and statistical evidence of biological efficacy. Many therapies have demonstrated robust treatment effects in relatively small, well‐conducted studies, raising the question of whether efficacy observed in ~150–200 patients should be discounted solely because it precedes a phase 3 trial enrolling ~1000 participants. The answer to this question is not purely scientific, but partly philosophical, and it helps explain variability across guideline recommendations. The choice between semaglutide and tirzepatide further illustrates the role of subjectivity in guideline development. A ‘purist’ approach may favour semaglutide based on phase 3 histologic data and regulatory approval for MASH. However, given the comparable magnitude of liver‐related effects in phase 2 MASH trials and head‐to‐head studies demonstrating greater reductions in HbA1c and body weight with tirzepatide, it is reasonable to infer similar hepatic benefits, particularly since much of the liver improvement appears to be weight‐loss mediated. Because semaglutide and tirzepatide are distinct molecules with different mechanisms of action, extrapolation must be cautious, yet the available data supports a clinically defensible approach in which both agents are considered broadly comparable from a liver perspective. Within this context, the debate surrounding agent selection during guideline development goes beyond biological efficacy. Evidence‐grading frameworks such as GRADE do not explicitly differentiate phase 2 from phase 3 trials, but they emphasise certainty of evidence, including risk of bias, consistency, and precision. Therefore, while phase 3 trials more readily support strong recommendations by virtue of larger sample size and narrower confidence intervals, phase 2 trials may support conditional recommendations based on moderate‐certainty evidence. Importantly, earlier MASH guidelines incorporated agents such as pioglitazone and vitamin E on the basis of consistent phase 2 histologic data, when phase 3 data was unavailable. In a similar manner, agents such as dapagliflozin and tirzepatide have demonstrated meaningful histologic signals in well‐designed phase 2 trials, , alongside well‐established benefits in metabolic, cardiovascular, and renal outcomes. Although these data may not meet the threshold for strong recommendations as MASH‐directed therapies, GRADE methodology allows for their consideration as conditional options with lower certainty of evidence, particularly in appropriately selected patients with relevant comorbidities. Taken together, this distinction highlights the complementary, but

earlier MASH guidelines incorporated agents such as pioglitazone and vitamin E on the basis of consistent phase 2 histologic data, when phase 3 data was unavailable. In a similar manner, agents such as dapagliflozin and tirzepatide have demonstrated meaningful histologic signals in well‐designed phase 2 trials, , alongside well‐established benefits in metabolic, cardiovascular, and renal outcomes. Although these data may not meet the threshold for strong recommendations as MASH‐directed therapies, GRADE methodology allows for their consideration as conditional options with lower certainty of evidence, particularly in appropriately selected patients with relevant comorbidities. Taken together, this distinction highlights the complementary, but non‐identical, roles of regulatory approval and clinical practice guidelines in translating evolving evidence into individualised patient care. The roles of SGLT‐2 inhibitors and pioglitazone further highlight discrepancies between hepatology‐ and endocrinology‐led guidance. These agents receive greater emphasis in AACE and ADA documents, , reflecting their proven benefits in diabetes, cardiovascular disease, chronic kidney disease, and heart failure. Given that proof of histological benefit on resolution of MASH and fibrosis improvement with dapagliflozin use is recent, SGLT‐2 inhibitors have not yet been incorporated into guidelines. Moreover, as standalone MASH‐targeted therapies, they still require replication in a Phase 3 trial. However, they are an instrumental part of the holistic management of individuals with CKM syndrome given their extensive benefits, especially in those at high cardiovascular risk. Unlike GLP‐1RA, their effects are likely not mediated by weight loss, making them an excellent possibility even in MASLD without increased adiposity. Pioglitazone, although supported by long‐standing histologic data and low cost, , , occupies an increasingly marginal role due to concerns about weight gain, edema, fractures, and potential malignancy risk. Nevertheless, given its cardiovascular benefits and liver efficacy that is numerically comparable to GLP‐1RA, , , pioglitazone remains a reasonable option in selected patients with diabetes, particularly where access to newer therapies is limited. Finally, when MASH is approached in a manner analogous to hypertension, dyslipidemia, or diabetes, it becomes evident that combination therapy will increasingly represent standard practice. Although guidelines generally endorse combining therapies when appropriate, they provide little direction on optimal sequencing beyond a preference for sequential rather than simultaneous initiation. As the field moves towards combination regimens targeting complementary pathways, future guidelines will need to move beyond single‐agent paradigms and more explicitly address how to integrate multiple therapies to maximise both hepatic and extrahepatic benefits. In line with this, a simplified algorithm of medication preference based on comorbidities (e.g., obesity, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, or heart failure) is provided in Figure . With current evidence, it would be premature to recommend simultaneous initiation of MASH‐directed therapies, given the lack of evidence. There is general consensus that monotherapy is preferred with consideration of additional medications based on monitoring after 12–18 months. , 10.3 Monitoring response to treatment After initiation of MASH‐directed pharmacotherapy, all current guidance agrees on the need for a monitoring strategy that is noninvasive, longitudinal, and anchored to the same NITs used to establish treatment eligibility, while also incorporating drug‐specific safety surveillance. Early follow‐up should prioritise assessment of tolerability and safety, particularly during dose escalation for incretin‐based therapies and through structured laboratory monitoring for resmetirom. Beyond early safety, efficacy assessment should focus on changes over time rather than absolute thresholds, recognising biological variability and the absence of fully validated on‐treatment cutoffs. Repeat fibrosis assessment using the same modality employed at baseline (e.g., VCTE, MRE, or ELF) is recommended to allow meaningful interpretation of trends, with reassessment typically performed at approximately 12 months for resmetirom or semaglutide , or even longer for semaglutide as recommended by AASLD (72 weeks consistent with the pivotal trial duration). Across documents, a clinically meaningful response is generally defined as a relative reduction in LSM exceeding expected test variability, commonly cited as a ≥25%–30% decrease in VCTE‐derived LSM or a ≥20% decrease in MRE, with supportive changes in liver enzymes, ELF score, or MRI‐PDFF when available. Improvement or stabilisation of fibrosis markers supports treatment continuation, whereas consistent worsening should prompt reassessment of adherence, metabolic control, and the possibility of disease progression or cirrhosis. Importantly, none of the guidelines recommend routine repeat liver biopsy for response monitoring; invasive reassessment is reserved for atypical or discordant cases. This flexible, trend‐based approach reflects both the limitations of current biomarkers and the evolving therapeutic landscape, emphasising individualised decision‐making over rigid stopping rules while maintaining a structured framework for longitudinal care (summarised in Figure ). 11 CONCLUSIONS Contemporary MASLD/MASH guidelines reflect a rapidly advancing field, with increasing reliance on noninvasive tests, expanding pharmacologic options, and growing recognition of the need for multidisciplinary care. Across documents, there is broad agreement on core principles, including targeted screening, prioritisation of cardiometabolic risk reduction, initiation of MASH‐directed therapy without mandatory liver biopsy, and longitudinal noninvasive monitoring. Nevertheless, substantial heterogeneity persists in how these principles are operationalised.

Across documents, there is broad agreement on core principles, including targeted screening, prioritisation of cardiometabolic risk reduction, initiation of MASH‐directed therapy without mandatory liver biopsy, and longitudinal noninvasive monitoring. Nevertheless, substantial heterogeneity persists in how these principles are operationalised. Differences in target populations for screening, NIT thresholds, treatment initiation strategies, and monitoring approaches often stem from reliance on trial‐derived populations, subjectivity in interpreting emerging evidence, and the rapid pace at which new data are generated relative to guideline update cycles. Future guidelines would benefit from greater transparency regarding areas where evidence remains limited or evolving, clearer integration of comorbidities into therapeutic decision‐making, and explicit consideration of cost and access. Moreover, guidance on therapy sequencing and combination strategies will be essential to address the growing burden of MASLD/MASH more effectively. documents.title: AASLD Practice Guidance on Alcohol Associated Liver Disease

chunks.content: 1 | INTRODUCTION Steatotic liver disease (SLD) develops into hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and liver decompensation. – Furthermore, SLD is associated with metabolic abnormalities and increases the risk of cardiovascular events. , SLD affects more than 25% of the global population, and it is posing an economic and health burden. Therefore, early detection of its complications and treatment to control them in patients with SLD are critical issues. The new nomenclature for SLD was recently been published, and it is classified as metabolic dysfunction-associated SLD (MASLD), MASLD and alcohol intake, or alcoholic liver disease, depending on the amount of alcohol consumed. Because the concordance rate between nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) and MASLD exceeds 95–99%, conventional NAFLD can be reclassified as MASLD. , NAFLD was diagnosed using exclusion criteria, whereas MASLD is diagnosed using inclusion criteria that include five cardiometabolic criteria (body mass index [BMI] or waist circumference, glucose, blood pressure, triglycerides, and high-density lipoprotein [HDL] cholesterol). These five criteria correspond to the diagnostic criteria for metabolic syndrome based on the consensus of several scientific committees. The identification of predictive markers and treatment targets for liver-related and cardiovascular events in patients with MASLD is a critical clinical issue that has not been adequately investigated. In particular, it is unclear whether the five cardiometabolic criteria are associated with the risk of liver-related and cardiovascular events and can be used as predictors and treatment targets for complications. To fill a current knowledge gap, we conducted this nationwide, population-based cohort study to investigate the relationship between cardiometabolic criteria and complications in patients with MASLD. 2 | METHODS 2.1 | Data source In this nationwide, population-based cohort study, we used a nationwide large claims database created by the Japan Medical Data Center (JMDC Co., Ltd. Tokyo, Japan). The database contains monthly claims from hospitals, tertiary centers, primary care facilities, and pharmacies. Medical and pharmacy claims include diagnosis, drug products, clinical procedure/treatment, materials, and Japan’s unique diagnosis procedure combination code for inpatients and outpatients. Diagnoses were coded using the International Classification of Diseases, 10th revision (ICD-10). When a patient dies, the database records the date of death as well as the corresponding ICD code associated with the disease that caused the death. Prescriptions were classified using the World Health Organization Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical classification system, which included the prescription date, daily dose per prescription, dose unit, number of days of administration per prescription, and dosage. The clinical practice data included examination, treatment, surgery, anaesthesia, and rehabilitation using Japan’s unique procedure/treatment code. Because the health insurance association integrated all claims, diagnosis and treatment were tracked even when patients changed care providers, allowing for an accurate long-term assessment of disease progression. – The database also contains the annual health checkup results for each case. The annual health checkup results include age, gender, physical examination, medical history, blood test results, and questionnaire data on smoking and alcohol consumption. Because companies are required by law to provide annual health checkups for their employees in Japan, health checkup data on cases not seen by any healthcare provider is also included, resulting in a more population-based dataset. The specifics of this database were shown in a previous report. 2.2 | Study protocol Currently, the database contains approximately 17 million patients from 2005 to 2023, and we investigated patients with annual health checkup data from the entire dataset. Among these cases, patients with SLD were discovered. The presence of SLD was defined by an ICD-10 code of K760 and/or fatty liver index >60. Exclusion criteria were as follows: (1) other chronic liver diseases, such as viral hepatitis, autoimmune hepatitis, primary biliary cholangitis, primary sclerosing cholangitis, and α1-antitrypsin deficiency; (2) excessive alcohol consumption; (3) history of HCC, hepatic decompensation, and major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE); and (4) patients who did not met cardiometabolic criteria (non MASLD). Finally, 979,352 patients with MASLD were included in the study. The patient selection process is illustrated in . provides detailed definitions for the inclusion and exclusion criteria. The initial health checkup date was used as a baseline, and the incidence of liver-related events and MACE was investigated. The study protocol conforms to the ethical guidelines of the Declaration of Helsinki, and the study was approved by the ethics committee of Musashino Red Cross Hospital (approval number: 5079). Because personal information was completely deleted from the database, the database had no personal information, and patient consent was not required. 2.3 | Definitions of liver-related events and MACE Liver-related events included HCC, ascites, variceal bleeding, hepatic encephalopathy, and death as a result of liver-related events. MACE was defined as a myocardial infarction, stroke, or cardiovascular death. These events were identified combining the diagnostic code (ICD-10) and the corresponding procedure/treatment ( ). For example, HCC was diagnosed using ICD-10 codes C220 or C227 and treated with radiofrequency ablation, liver resection, transcatheter

committee of Musashino Red Cross Hospital (approval number: 5079). Because personal information was completely deleted from the database, the database had no personal information, and patient consent was not required. 2.3 | Definitions of liver-related events and MACE Liver-related events included HCC, ascites, variceal bleeding, hepatic encephalopathy, and death as a result of liver-related events. MACE was defined as a myocardial infarction, stroke, or cardiovascular death. These events were identified combining the diagnostic code (ICD-10) and the corresponding procedure/treatment ( ). For example, HCC was diagnosed using ICD-10 codes C220 or C227 and treated with radiofrequency ablation, liver resection, transcatheter arterial chemoembolisation, or chemotherapy (sorafenib, lenvatinib, regorafenib, ramucirumab, cabozantinib, or atezolizumab plus bevacizumab). The combination of diagnosis codes and procedure/treatment had a sensitivity of 93% and specificity of 100% for diagnosing specific conditions, outperforming ICD-10 alone. 2.4 | Cardiometabolic criteria The five cardiometabolic criteria (BMI or waist circumference, glucose, blood pressure, triglycerides, and HDL cholesterol) were examined using health checkup results, and the number of criteria met was determined. The definition of each criterion as follows: BMI ≥23 kg/m 2 (Asian) or waist circumference >94 cm for males and 80 cm for females; fasting glucose ≥100 mg/dL or HbA1c ≥5.7% or type 2 diabetes or treatment for type 2 diabetes; blood pressure ≥130/85 mmHg or specific antihypertensive drug treatment; plasma triglycerides ≥150 mg/dL or lipid-lowering treatment; plasma HDL-cholesterol ≤40 mg/dL for males and 50 mg/dL for females or lipid-lowering treatment. Furthermore, because health checkups are performed annually, the number of criteria met was surveyed every year for up to 10 years. Longitudinal studies were evaluated based on the average of the criteria surveyed every year between 1 and 10 years or until an event occurred. 2.5 | Primary endpoint The study’s primary outcome was the relationship between the number of criteria met and liver-related events and MACE risks. The first study investigated the relationship between the number of criteria met at the start of observation and the risk of developing complications, as well as whether the number of criteria met could be used to predict complications. We then investigated the relationship between improved criteria and the risk of complications. Only patients who met all five criteria at the start of observation were included in the longitudinal study, which looked at the number of criteria met at follow-up (median number of criteria between follow-up) and the development of complications. We investigated whether improved criteria were associated with a lower risk of complication occurrence and could be used as treatment goals. The study design is depicted in . 2.6 | Statistical analyses The cumulative incidence of liver-related events and MACE was investigated using the Kaplan–Meier method and the log-rank test. The multivariable analysis was performed using the Cox proportional hazard model to calculate the adjusted hazard ratio (aHR) with a 95% confidence interval (CI) for liver-related events and MACE. For the multivariable analysis, factors such as age, gender, current smoking status, and the number of cardiometabolic criteria were predetermined covariates. This data on covariables was collected for all patients, and no data was missing. Statistical significance was defined as p -values of <0.05. All statistical analyses were conducted using EZR (Saitama Medical Center, Jichi Medical University, Shimotsuke, Japan), a graphical user interface for R version 3.2.2 (The R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria). 3 | RESULTS 3.1 | Patient characteristics The study included 979,352 patients with MASLD ( ). The median (interquartile range [IQR]) age was 44 (37–52) years, and 76.6% were men. The prevalence of diabetes mellitus (DM), dyslipidemia, and hypertension (HT) was 20.3%, 70.8%, and 34.2%, respectively. According to the cardiometabolic criteria, patients who met one, two, three, four, and five were 13.3%, 13.8%, 21.6%, 23.6%, and 27.7%, respectively. The median (IQR) follow-up periods were 5.2 (3.3–7.2) years and during the follow-up 670 patients and 11,328 patients developed liver-related events and MACE, respectively. 3.2 | Baseline cardiometabolic criteria and risk of liver-related events First, we investigated the relationship between baseline cardio-metabolic criteria and the incidence of liver-related events. In patients who fulfilled one, two, three, four, and five cardiometabolic criteria, the 3-, 5-, and 10-year incidence of liver-related events were 0.002%, 0.02%, and 0.06% for patients with 1 criterion, 0.01%, 0.05%, and 0.10% for patients with two criteria, 0.01%, 0.04%, and 0.08% for patients with 3 criteria, 0.02%, 0.04%, and 0.12% for patients with 4 criteria, and 0.04%, 0.12%, and 0.25% for patients with 5 criteria, respectively ( ). The incidence was significantly higher in patients with 5 criteria than others ( p < 0.001) and significantly lower in patients with 1 criterion compared to those with 2, 4, and 5 criteria ( p = 0.02, 0.006, and <0.001). There was no significant difference between patients with 2, 3, and 4 criteria. A multivariable analysis adjusting for age, gender,

0.01%, 0.05%, and 0.10% for patients with two criteria, 0.01%, 0.04%, and 0.08% for patients with 3 criteria, 0.02%, 0.04%, and 0.12% for patients with 4 criteria, and 0.04%, 0.12%, and 0.25% for patients with 5 criteria, respectively ( ). The incidence was significantly higher in patients with 5 criteria than others ( p < 0.001) and significantly lower in patients with 1 criterion compared to those with 2, 4, and 5 criteria ( p = 0.02, 0.006, and <0.001). There was no significant difference between patients with 2, 3, and 4 criteria. A multivariable analysis adjusting for age, gender, smoking, and cardiometabolic criteria revealed that the aHRs (95% CI) of liver-related events in patients with 2, 3, 4, and 5 criteria (using patients with 1 criterion as the reference) were 1.22 (0.8–1.7, p = 0.3), 1.00 (0.7–1.4, p = 0.9), 0.93 (0.7–1.3, p = 0.7), and 1.63 (1.2–2.2, p = 0.003), respectively. The risk of liver-related events was high in patients with 5 criteria, but there was no significant difference between patients with 1, 2, 3, and 4 criteria ( ). 3.3 | Baseline cardiometabolic criteria and risk of MACE Next, we investigated the relationship between baseline cardiometabolic criteria and the incidence of MACE. In patients who fulfilled 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 cardiometabolic criteria, the 3-, 5-, and 10-year incidence of MACE were 0.1%, 0.2%, and 0.4% for patients with 1 criterion, 0.2%, 0.4%, and 1.0% for patients with 2 criteria, 0.2%, 0.5%, and 1.3% for patients with 3 criteria, 0.5%, 0.9%, and 2.3% for patients with 4 criteria, and 1.2%, 2.2%, and 4.7% for patients with 5 criteria, respectively ( ). The incidence of MACE increased with increasing cardiometabolic criteria ( p < 0.001 between all two groups). Multivariable analysis adjusting age, gender, smoking, and cardiometabolic criteria revealed that aHRs (95% CI) of MACE in patients with 2, 3, 4, and 5 criteria (using patients with 1 criterion as the reference) were 1.66 (1.5–1.9, p < 0.001), 1.84 (1.6–2.1, p < 0.001), 2.79 (2.5–3.1, p < 0.001), and 5.00 (4.5–5.6, p < 0.001), respectively. The risk of MACE increased as the cardiometabolic criteria increased ( ). 3.4 | Improvement of cardiometabolic criteria and risk of liver-related events In patients with five cardiometabolic criteria at baseline, the relationship between improvement in the criteria and the incidence of liver-related events after 1 year of observation was investigated. An average number of cardiometabolic criteria between 1 and 10 years or until an event occurred was counted and used for the analysis. In patients with 0–1 criterion (4–5 criteria improvement), 2 criteria (3 criteria improvement), 3 criteria (2 criteria improvement), 4 criteria (1 criterion improvement), and 5 criteria (no improvement), the 3-, 5-, and 10-year incidence of liver-related events were 0.07%, 0.07%, and 0.07% for patients with 0–1 criterion, 0.06%, 0.1%, and 0.2% for patients with 2 criteria, 0.06%, 0.1%, and 0.3% for patients with 3 criteria, 0.04%, 0.09%, and 0.2% for patients with 4 criteria, and 0.05%, 0.1%, and 0.2% for patients with 5 criteria, respectively ( ). No significant differences were found between the two groups. Multivariable analysis adjusting age, gender, smoking, and improved cardiometabolic criteria demonstrated that there was no significant relation between the risk of liver-related events and improvement in cardiometabolic criteria ( ). 3.5 | Improvement of cardiometabolic criteria and risk of MACE In patients with 5 cardiometabolic criteria at baseline, the relationship between improvement in the criteria and the incidence of MACE after 1 year of observation was also investigated. In patients with 0–1 criterion (4–5 criteria improvement), 2 criteria (3 criteria improvement), 3 criteria (2 criteria improvement), 4 criteria (1 criterion improvement), and 5 criteria (no improvement), the 3-, 5-, and 10-year incidence of MACE were 0.2%, 0.2%, and 0.2% for patients with 0–1 criterion, 0.1%, 0.3%, and 0.8% for patients with 2 criteria, 0.2%, 0.5%, and 1.6% for patients with 3 criteria, 0.7%, 1.6%, and 4.1% for patients with 4 criteria, and 1.7%, 3.3%, and 7.3% for patients with 5 criteria, respectively ( ). Improved cardiometabolic criteria led to a decrease in MACE incidence ( p < 0.001 across both groups). Multivariable analysis adjusting age, gender, smoking, and improved cardiometabolic criteria demonstrated that adjusted HRs (95% CI) of MACE in patients with 4, 3, 2, and 0–1 criteria (patients with 5 criteria [no improvement] using as the reference) were 0.55 (0.52–0.58, p < 0.001), 0.20 (0.17–0.22, p < 0.001), 0.13 (0.11–0.16, p < 0.001), and 0.06 (0.02–0.26, p < 0.001), respectively ( ). The risk of MACE decreased as cardiometabolic criteria improved. 4 | DISCUSSION 4.1 | Main findings In this nationwide, population-based cohort study of 979,352 patients with MASLD, we found that increasing the cardiometabolic criteria increased the risk of MACE while improving the cardiometabolic criteria reduced the risk of MACE.

that adjusted HRs (95% CI) of MACE in patients with 4, 3, 2, and 0–1 criteria (patients with 5 criteria [no improvement] using as the reference) were 0.55 (0.52–0.58, p < 0.001), 0.20 (0.17–0.22, p < 0.001), 0.13 (0.11–0.16, p < 0.001), and 0.06 (0.02–0.26, p < 0.001), respectively ( ). The risk of MACE decreased as cardiometabolic criteria improved. 4 | DISCUSSION 4.1 | Main findings In this nationwide, population-based cohort study of 979,352 patients with MASLD, we found that increasing the cardiometabolic criteria increased the risk of MACE while improving the cardiometabolic criteria reduced the risk of MACE. In contrast, the risk of liver-related events was not associated with baseline cardiometabolic criteria, except in patients with 5 criteria, or with improvement in cardiometabolic criteria. Therefore, in patients with MASLD, the cardiometabolic criteria could be used as predictors and treatment targets for MACE, but other factors indicating the risk of liver-related events should be investigated in the future. 4.2 | In context with published literature MASLD increases the risk of liver-related events and MACE. In patients with MASLD, the incidence of MACE is more common than that of liver-related events, so preventing them is critical. Although metabolic diseases such as DM, dyslipidemia, and HT are risk factors for MACE, the relationship between cardiometabolic criteria of MASLD and the risk of MACE in MASLD patients is unclear. In this study, we found that increasing the cardiometabolic criteria increased the risk of MACE. Therefore, the cardiometabolic criteria are valid for predicting cardiovascular event risk. Another important consideration is whether these criteria can serve as treatment targets. Guidelines for NAFLD/MASLD recommend treating metabolic disorders but do not specify treatment targets/goals to prevent complications. – In this study, we showed that controlling metabolic diseases (BMI, waist circumference, blood pressure, glucose, HDL, and TG) within the criteria can help prevent cardiovascular events, and thus the criteria can be used as therapeutic targets. MASLD is a risk factor for liver-related events, so the link between the criteria and liver-related events should also be investigated. However, when examining the association between cardiometabolic criteria and liver-related events, this study found no significant association. Therefore, the cardiometabolic criteria cannot be used to predict and treat liver-related events. The presence of DM in patients with MASLD is known to increase the risk of liver-related events, and we previously reported that the optimal HbA1c level to prevent liver-related events is <7%, while patients with HbA1c levels <5% have also a high risk of liver-related events. , , In contrast, the MASLD criteria for glucose are fasting glucose ≥100 mg/dL or HbA1c ≥5.7%. As the difference in thresholds may affect the risk of liver-related events, an optimal threshold to prevent liver-related events may need to be validated. In patients with chronic liver disease, glucose, cholesterol, and blood pressure levels fall as liver fibrosis progresses to cirrhosis and decompensation. , This phenomenon could explain why no association was found between the criteria and liver-related events. The presence of DM is the risk factor for liver-related events in MASLD. , However, it is still unclear whether improved glucose or HbA1c levels in patients with DM are associated with improved risk of liver-related events. It is also unclear whether there is a difference in the effect of DM medications on the risk of liver-related events. Further validation of these points is needed. Because liver fibrosis is the most common risk factor of liver-related events, liver fibrosis assessment, rather than cardiometabolic criteria, is required to assess the risk of liver-related events. – Furthermore, the treatment goal for reducing liver-related events should be to improve liver fibrosis rather than the cardiometabolic criterion. 4.3 | Strengths and limitations This nationwide, population-based cohort study included 979,352 patients with MASLD. In Japan, companies are required by law to provide annual health checkups to their employees, which include physical measurements and blood tests, and this study database is based on health checkup results and claim data. Therefore, this database includes cases that have not been seen by any health-care provider, making it more suitable for population analyses. Furthermore, because the health insurance association integrated all claims, diagnosis, and treatment were tracked even when patients switched care providers, allowing for an accurate long-term assessment of disease progression. Liver-related events and MACE were defined using the diagnostic code (ICD-10) and the corresponding procedure/treatment. The combination of diagnosis codes and procedure/treatment had a specificity of 100% for diagnosing specific conditions, outperforming ICD-10 alone. Because this study/database focuses on relatively young male cases, more research is needed in cohorts that include elderly patients or females. 4.4 | Future implications The prevention of complications such as liver-related events and MACE in MASLD is critical, but predictors and treatment targets have yet to be established. In this study, we found that increasing the cardiometabolic criteria increased

accurate long-term assessment of disease progression. Liver-related events and MACE were defined using the diagnostic code (ICD-10) and the corresponding procedure/treatment. The combination of diagnosis codes and procedure/treatment had a specificity of 100% for diagnosing specific conditions, outperforming ICD-10 alone. Because this study/database focuses on relatively young male cases, more research is needed in cohorts that include elderly patients or females. 4.4 | Future implications The prevention of complications such as liver-related events and MACE in MASLD is critical, but predictors and treatment targets have yet to be established. In this study, we found that increasing the cardiometabolic criteria increased the risk of MACE while improving the cardiometabolic criteria reduced the risk. Therefore, cardiometabolic criteria can serve as predictors and treatment targets for cardiovascular event risk in patients with MASLD. Because clear treatment targets for metabolic diseases (target values for glucose, cholesterol, and blood pressure) in MASLD have yet to be defined, these criteria could be used as treatment targets for MACE, which is clinically significant. In contrast, there was no link discovered between the criteria and liver-related events. Different thresholds for metabolic diseases may need to be validated to reduce liver-related events. Liver feature assessment including fibrosis or steatosis may also be useful for determining the risk of liver-related events in MASLD. – Developing predictive markers and therapeutic targets for the risk of liver-related events in MASLD is a significant future challenge. To summarise, increasing the cardiometabolic criteria increased the risk of MACE, while improving the cardiometabolic criteria reduced the risk. In contrast, the risk of liver-related events was not linked to baseline cardiometabolic criteria. Cardiometabolic criteria can be used as predictors and treatment targets for cardiovascular event risk, but developing predictive markers and therapeutic targets for liver-related events is a significant future challenge. documents.title: AASLD Practice Guidance on Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis

chunks.content: INTRODUCTION Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) is a chronic cholestatic liver disease marked by progressive inflammation and fibrosis of the intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts, eventually leading to cirrhosis and liver failure. Its incidence is estimated 0.6–0.9 per 100,000 person-years, with a prevalence of up to ∼13 per 100,000 persons in Western populations and with a male predominance. Pathogenesis remains unclear and diagnosis relies on cholestatic liver tests, imaging features and exclusion of secondary causes. In the peripartum period, diagnosis is challenging, as pregnancy-related hormonal changes can alter bile composition, liver enzyme levels, and hepatic excretory capacity, and intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy (ICP) may confound interpretation of cholestatic liver disease. Other conditions such as drug-induced liver injury (DILI) or gallbladder disease may further obscure recognition of underlying PSC. However, reports of PSC first presenting or flaring after pregnancy are limited. We present a postpartum case of severe, progressive cholestasis initially attributed to ICP, gallstone-pancreatitis, and cephalexin-induced liver injury. The ultimate diagnosis of PSC was only achieved after serial imaging, biopsy, and endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP). This case illustrates postpartum evolution of PSC and underscores the need for reassessment when cholestasis persists. CASE REPORT 26-week gestation—Initial presentation A 36-year-old G2P0010 woman at presentation, with polycystic ovarian syndrome, anxiety, prolactinoma, gestational hypertension, and prior Helicobacter pylori infection, and no substance use history, presented at 26 weeks gestation with acute epigastric and right upper quadrant pain, nausea, and vomiting. Laboratory results showed lipase 648 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase (AST) 38 U/L, alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 28 U/L, alkaline phosphatase (ALP) 105 U/L, and total bilirubin (TB) 4.3 mg/dL (reference range 0.4–1.5 mg/dL). Imaging revealed gallbladder sludge without cholecystitis on ultrasound, and acute pancreatitis with peripancreatic edema and gallbladder wall edema on magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP), without choledocholithiasis or obstruction. She was managed supportively and discharged with improving liver tests. Given her episode of gallstone pancreatitis and gallbladder sludge, interval cholecystectomy was planned; however, the procedure was deferred due to progressive cholestatic liver injury. She ultimately did not undergo cholecystectomy. 32–37-week gestation—Development of ICP After discharge, between 32 and 37 weeks gestation, liver tests worsened; ALP peaked at 378 U/L and at TB 5.4 mg/dL, and she developed pruritus. Serum bile acids were elevated at 77 µmol/L, exceeding the diagnostic threshold for ICP. Secondary causes, including biliary obstruction and viral hepatitis, were excluded, and ICP was favored based on late-gestation onset, symptoms, and elevated bile acids. Ursodiol (9 mg/kg/d) initiation at 32 weeks led to initial symptom improvement, supporting the diagnosis. Persistently elevated bilirubin and ALP prompted induction at 37 weeks. Ursodiol was stopped postpartum. Postpartum day 4—Readmission for recurrent cholestasis She initially felt well but was readmitted postpartum day 4 with right upper quadrant abdominal pain, jaundice, nausea, and vomiting. Laboratory results revealed AST 155, ALT 88, TB 5, and ALP 952. MRI showed a decompressed gallbladder with no biliary ductal dilatation or choledocholithiasis. At that time, no dominant strictures or intrahepatic ductal irregularities were identified, suggesting either early or evolving biliary disease below the threshold of MRCP detection. Serologic workup revealed a low titer antinuclear antibody (1:160); negative hepatitis A, B, and C; and negative anti-smooth muscle (SM) antibody and anti-mitochondrial antibodies (AMA). At 36-week gestation, she completed a 7-day course of cephalexin (500 mg every 6 hours) for an ear cellulitis. The antibiotic course was completed before delivery; she received no antibiotics during delivery and took only prenatal vitamins during pregnancy before starting ursodiol. Given the temporal proximity of cephalexin exposure to worsening cholestatic liver tests in the postpartum period, cephalexin-associated drug-induced liver injury was initially considered. Postpartum weeks 8–12—Evolution of biliary disease Her liver tests continued to rise (AST 127, ALT 98, TB 9.9, ALP 1,042) during her weeklong hospitalization. EUS was unremarkable, but liver biopsy demonstrated patchy cholestasis, lobular inflammation, and periportal fibrosis (Metavir stage F2) suggestive of DILI or viral hepatitis, and no features of primary biliary cholangitis, PSC, or autoimmune hepatitis (AIH). Although symptoms improved, upon discharge, TB increased to 11.5. Cholestyramine was started; however, it stopped after 1 week due to abdominal pain. Over the next 2 weeks, laboratory results worsened, and she developed intense pruritus and jaundice, prompting restart of ursodiol (13 mg/kg/d). At follow-up, AST, ALT, and ALP showed gradual improvement after 3 weeks of ursodiol, although bilirubin continued to rise. Ursodiol dose was reduced (10 mg/kg/d) due to diarrhea. Overall, ursodiol dosing was escalated postpartum (13 mg/kg/d) after antenatal initiation (9 mg/kg/d) and later reduced (10 mg/kg/d) due to gastrointestinal intolerance. Two weeks later, AST and ALT had improved further, but TB increased to 24, and ALP began to worsen again (Figures and ), despite prolonged avoidance of the presumed offending agent. Owing to concern for alternative etiologies, repeat MRCP and liver biopsy were performed. MRCP showed peribiliary hyperenhancement with peripherally dilated, irregular, and discontinuous bile

ALP showed gradual improvement after 3 weeks of ursodiol, although bilirubin continued to rise. Ursodiol dose was reduced (10 mg/kg/d) due to diarrhea. Overall, ursodiol dosing was escalated postpartum (13 mg/kg/d) after antenatal initiation (9 mg/kg/d) and later reduced (10 mg/kg/d) due to gastrointestinal intolerance. Two weeks later, AST and ALT had improved further, but TB increased to 24, and ALP began to worsen again (Figures and ), despite prolonged avoidance of the presumed offending agent. Owing to concern for alternative etiologies, repeat MRCP and liver biopsy were performed. MRCP showed peribiliary hyperenhancement with peripherally dilated, irregular, and discontinuous bile ducts, suggestive of PSC or diffuse bacterial cholangitis (Figure ). Biopsy revealed severe lobular cholestasis, feathery degeneration, focal hepatocyte dropout, periportal and patchy perisinusoidal fibrosis, mild portal neutrophilic and lymphoplasmacytic inflammation with ductular reaction, and bile duct injury (Figure ), consistent with a biliary process. Comparison with prior biopsy showed progression of chronic cholestatic liver injury with more fibrosis. Although features of biliary obstruction were present, classic findings of PSC (onion-skinning, ductopenia, bile duct proliferation) were absent, and disease progression prompted further evaluation. ERCP and definitive diagnosis ERCP was performed for further biliary evaluation. It demonstrated multifocal severe diffuse stenoses of the right and left intrahepatic bile duct branches, with irregularity of the main hepatic ducts. Mild stenoses were present in the proximal extrahepatic bile duct without a dominant stricture (maximum duct diameter 7 mm), consistent with large-duct PSC (Figure ). Bile duct brushings showed benign reactive ductal cells, consistent with PSC. Secondary causes were ruled out with negative COVID polymerase chain reaction and negative evaluation for autoimmune cholangiopathy (immunoglobulin G4 [IgG4] stain on liver biopsy negative, serum IgG4 normal at 12.3 mg/dL). Given the strong association between PSC and inflammatory bowel disease, colonoscopy was performed and showed no endoscopic or histologic evidence of inflammatory bowel disease. Final clinical course and transplantation At diagnosis, Model for End-Stage Liver Disease (MELD) 3.0 was 25. Over the next 3 months, fatigue, jaundice, and diarrhea persisted, with bilirubin > 20. Owing to ongoing liver dysfunction, she was evaluated and listed for transplant 6 months after ERCP (MELD 3.0: 29, driven by elevated bilirubin). Three weeks after listing (10 months postpartum), she underwent uncomplicated orthotopic liver transplant. Explant pathology demonstrated established cirrhosis with prominent bile staining and dilatation of intrahepatic bile ducts. Trichrome staining highlighted cirrhosis with occasional periductal fibrosis, while immunohistochemical staining for CK7 and CK19 showed extensive bile ductular proliferation and expansion of intermediate hepatocytes. There was no evidence of ductopenia, steatohepatitis, alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency, iron overload, or malignancy. Although classic fibrous obliterative cholangitis (“onion-skinning”) was not identified, the overall histologic findings, in conjunction with the patient's clinical course and cholangiographic features, were most consistent with PSC. She remains well with normal allograft function almost 6 months post-transplant. DISCUSSION This case highlights the diagnostic complexity of cholestatic liver disease in the postpartum period, where overlapping physiologic, drug-related, and biliary processes may mask PSC. The patient's history of ICP, gallstone pancreatitis, and recent cephalexin exposure introduced several confounders. Persistent liver enzyme elevations postpartum suggested DILI or another disorder, while biliary sludge or transient postpancreatitis cholestasis were also considered. Cephalexin was initially presumed to cause DILI given its known cholestatic pattern and latency of 1 to 4 weeks. Early MRCP and biopsy were nondiagnostic, showing no ductal dilation and histology with patchy cholestasis, mild inflammation, and periportal fibrosis, findings compatible with resolving injury without features characteristic of PSC, primary biliary cholangitis, or AIH, supporting a working DILI diagnosis. Ongoing symptoms and lack of laboratory improvement 10 weeks after antibiotic discontinuation prompted repeat MRCP and biopsy, which revealed progressive cholestatic changes and ductal irregularities consistent with chronic biliary disease not initially detectable on imaging. Early PSC may lack overt cholangiographic abnormalities on MRCP, particularly when disease is predominantly intrahepatic or inflammatory rather than fibrotic, which may explain the initially nondiagnostic imaging in this case. ERCP ultimately confirmed multifocal intrahepatic biliary strictures, highlighting the value of advanced endoscopic evaluation when noninvasive tests are inconclusive. In addition, although the antinuclear antibody was positive at a titer of 1:160, AIH-PSC overlap was considered unlikely given negative anti-SM antibody testing, absence of interface hepatitis or plasma cell infiltrates on biopsy, and a predominantly cholestatic clinical course. Consistent with this presentation, pregnancy may worsen established PSC and has been hypothesized to unmask previously subclinical disease. Elevated estrogen levels reduce bile flow through effects on bile acid signaling pathways, while higher progesterone levels slow smooth muscle contractions in the bile ducts and intestine. , , Sujana Kumar et al and Alruzaihan et al reported cases of PSC presenting during pregnancy with persistent cholestasis and progression to cirrhosis or hepatic decompensation, with disease persistence or worsening postpartum despite ursodiol therapy. , Several case reports also describe de novo PSC manifesting in otherwise healthy

and a predominantly cholestatic clinical course. Consistent with this presentation, pregnancy may worsen established PSC and has been hypothesized to unmask previously subclinical disease. Elevated estrogen levels reduce bile flow through effects on bile acid signaling pathways, while higher progesterone levels slow smooth muscle contractions in the bile ducts and intestine. , , Sujana Kumar et al and Alruzaihan et al reported cases of PSC presenting during pregnancy with persistent cholestasis and progression to cirrhosis or hepatic decompensation, with disease persistence or worsening postpartum despite ursodiol therapy. , Several case reports also describe de novo PSC manifesting in otherwise healthy women during or soon after pregnancy. Slade et al reported PSC presenting as liver dysfunction during pregnancy that worsened postpartum, culminating in liver transplantation within 1 year, while Hedda et al and Conte et al emphasized the importance of considering PSC when pregnancy-related cholestasis persists beyond delivery. – PSC may be associated with maternal and fetal complications, including higher rates of cholestasis flares, preterm delivery, and adverse perinatal outcomes in women with established PSC. , Collectively, these reports illustrate the heterogeneity of PSC presentation in the peripartum period. Unlike most reported cases in which PSC is either established before pregnancy or recognized late after delivery, this case demonstrates rapid postpartum evolution from nondiagnostic imaging to overt large-duct disease within a relatively short interval. Compared with these reports, our patient's course was more protracted, with progressive cholestasis evolving months after delivery. Early manifestations initially masqueraded as ICP or DILI before the chronic nature of disease became apparent. Although ERCP-confirmed structuring occurred several weeks postpartum, biochemical cholestasis preceded imaging changes and evolved gradually over 8–12 weeks. Despite progression to liver transplantation within 1 year of diagnosis, this course reflected accelerated cholestatic decompensation rather than fulminant disease. MELD 3.0 increased from 25 at diagnosis to 29 at listing, driven predominantly by progressive hyperbilirubinemia, with preserved renal function, stable international normalized ratio, and no hepatic encephalopathy or circulatory failure. This apparent tempo warrants consideration of pregnancy as a potential modifier of disease expression. The temporal association with pregnancy raises the possibility that PSC in this patient was subclinical before pregnancy or precipitated into clinical expression by pregnancy-related physiologic stressors. Early postpartum liver biopsy demonstrated periportal fibrosis, suggesting chronic cholestatic injury that may have predated pregnancy. However, pregnancy itself may act as a trigger that unmasks or accelerates previously compensated disease. Hormonal changes during pregnancy, including elevated estrogen-mediated impairment of bile flow and progesterone-related biliary hypomotility, may exacerbate biliary inflammation and cholestasis in susceptible individuals. Thus, the observed course likely reflects unmasking and amplification of underlying PSC rather than de novo rapidly progressive disease. Pancreatitis may have transiently affected cholestatic markers, further complicating interpretation and contributing to diagnostic delay. These observations underscore the need for vigilance and longitudinal follow-up in postpartum cholestasis when liver enzymes remain abnormal. Although no genetic testing for bile acid channel disorders (i.e., progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis [PFIC] variants, cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator [CFTR] mutations) was performed, such testing may have been informative given the patient's history of pancreatitis. This case offers several practical lessons for clinical management. Clinicians should maintain a low threshold for early reassessment when bilirubin persists or rises despite improving aminotransferases to prevent progression to advanced liver disease or the need for transplantation. Repeat liver testing and imaging (e.g., MRCP) should be pursued if bilirubin or ALP remain elevated beyond 4–6 weeks postpartum. Progressive cholestasis or inconclusive imaging warrants early hepatology referral and consideration of ERCP, particularly in the setting of worsening hyperbilirubinemia, pruritus, or evolving ductal irregularities. A systematic approach that emphasizes serial monitoring and timely escalation to endoscopic evaluation can facilitate earlier recognition of PSC and allow for appropriate disease management or transplant planning. Overall, this case reinforces the importance of vigilance, multidisciplinary collaboration, and proactive evaluation in postpartum patients with atypical or prolonged cholestasis. chunks.content: Introduction Primary liver cancer (PLC) is the sixth most common malignancy in the world and the third most common cancer-related mortality [ , ]. Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), being the predominant subtype of PLC, constitutes approximately 90 % of all primary liver cancers [ ]. Additionally, HCC is also one of the most common malignant tumors in China, ranking fifth in the incidence of malignant tumors in China, and second in mortality [ , ]. HCC is characterized by high malignancy and easy metastasis [ ] Currently, surgical resection is the most efficacious treatment for HCC [ ]. Despite remarkable progress in diagnosis, surgical treatment, and adjuvant therapy, the prognosis for HCC remains unfavorable due to frequent recurrence and metastasis [ ]. Studies have shown that about 50 %−70 % of HCC patients experience recurrences and metastases within 5 years after surgery, and 70 % of patients encounter recurrences within 2 years [ ]. Consequently, high postoperative tumor recurrence and metastases hinder the improvement of the prognosis of liver cancer patients [ ]. The poor prognosis of liver cancer is the result of a series of processes such as proliferation, extracellular matrix remodeling, angiogenesis, and microenvironment [ ]. It is still difficult to accurately predict the risk factors related to patient prognosis. The important indicators used to predict the prognosis of liver cancer encompass serum Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) concentration, clinical stage, microvascular infiltration degree, tumor differentiation degree, etc [ ]. However, due to the high heterogeneity in liver cancer, the sensitivity and specificity of alpha-fetoprotein in the diagnosis of liver cancer are relatively limited [ , ]. About one-third of HCC patients have negative serum AFP from the beginning, and AFP is also elevated in people at high risk of liver cancer. Even among liver cancer cases with the same tumor stage, different patients often have different prognosis and treatment effects, which is the intricate interplay of multiple factors, so neither serum AFP concentration nor tumor stage can meet the prognosis assessment and management of liver cancer [ , ]. Therefore, it has become an urgent need to explore new diagnostic genes and prognostic markers for liver cancer to enhance the clinical therapeutic effect and improve the postoperative prognosis of patients. Tumor microenvironment (TME) assumes a crucial role in the occurrence and development of liver cancer, which not only participates in tumor progression but also influences the prognosis of HCC patients [ ]. It has been reported that tumor microenvironment coexists and interacts with various immune cells. To maintain the development of HCC, the dysfunctional tumor immune ecosystem may precipitate the breakdown of immune surveillance. Immunosuppression of TME is the external cause of the immune escape of HCC [ , ]. It has also been found that the effectiveness of immunotherapy largely depends on the tumor immune microenvironment (TIME) [ ]. Exploring the molecular mechanisms of TME can enhance our understanding of the mechanisms involved in tumor development and contribute to the discovery of more effective treatment strategies for HCC [ ]. TME is a complex ecosystem containing a variety of cell types, cytokines, and extracellular matrix (ECM), which play an important role in the carcinogenesis and therapeutic effectiveness of malignant tumors [ , ]. However, various types of immune cells play an important role in the tumor microenvironment. Although the proportion and importance of each cell infiltrating cancer tissue varies by case and tissue type, macrophages have always been the dominant cell, playing an important role in cancer tissue [ ] and have been proven to be associated with poor tumor prognosis [ ]. Macrophages are classic multifunctional immune cells, which are capable of eliminating tumor cells through innate immune response and act as antigen-presenting cells, activate adaptive immunity, and produce anti-tumor effects [ ]. Macrophages are the main components of immune cells in the tumor microenvironment [ ]. Macrophages can be polarized into two forms, M1 and M2. M1 macrophages promote inflammation and target tumor cells by secreting a large number of pro-inflammatory factors. M2 macrophages play a role in anti-inflammatory, damaged tissue recovery, and tumor promotion [ ]. In early-stage cancer, tumor-associated macrophages (Tumor-Associated-Macrophages, TAM) predominantly manifest as M1 macrophages. However, with the progression of cancer, M1 macrophages undergo polarization to the M2 subtype [ ]. In the tumor microenvironment, M2-type TAMs promote tumor invasion, metastasis, and immunosuppression by inducing angiogenesis, assisting tumor cells to escape immune surveillance, and degrading tumor extracellular matrix [ ]. In summary, macrophages play an important role in the occurrence and development of liver cancer, especially M2-type macrophages are of great value in predicting the prognosis of liver cancer [ ]. However, the specific mechanism of macrophages in the occurrence and development of liver cancer is not fully understood, which we speculate may be related to the differential expression of macrophage-related regulatory genes. To this end, we conducted a preliminary study on the gene expression differences between HCC macrophages and para-cancer macrophages by single-cell sequencing. In this study, single-cell sequencing data: GSE149614 , hepatocellular carcinoma transcriptome 1: GDC TCGA Liver Cancer (LIHC), hepatocellular carcinoma transcriptome 2: Single-cell data analysis was performed in the GSE145203 database to screen out significantly upregulated macrophage markers. We investigated the function of 20 significantly upregulated macrophage markers in this research. We found that FCGR2A is mainly expressed in M2 macrophages of HCC. However, the function and mechanism of FCGR2A in macrophages remain unclear. Therefore, we designed this study to further verify the relationship between FCGR2A and postoperative prognosis of HCC patients by histopathology. Materials and methods HCC tissue collection A retrospective analysis was performed on 185 patients who received partial hepatectomy in our hospital for the first time from April 2020 to July 2021, and 80 patients were included in the study according to the exclusion criteria. Inclusion criteria: (1) Pathological diagnosis of primary hepatocellular carcinoma after surgical resection; (2) The first tumor treatment after admission was surgical treatment. Exclusion criteria: (1) Liver metastases from other malignant tumors or other malignant tumors at the same time; (2) Received local therapy, systemic chemotherapy, targeted therapy, and other treatments before surgery; (3) Lack of patient data and incomplete follow-up data. Paraffin-embedded HCC specimens, including cancer tissues and adjacent tissues, were selected from enrolled patients in the pathology department of our hospital for subsequent immunofluorescence chemical staining and immunohistochemical staining. Clinicopathological data include: Patient age, patient sex, tissue AFP, serum AFP, tumor size and number, lymph node and distant metastasis, Portal vein tumor thrombus, PVTT, China National Logging Corporation (CNLC), differentiation degree, Microvascular Invasion (MVI), satellite nodules, etc. All the experiments were carried out under a Human Research Ethics Committees protocol at Yunnan Cancer Hospital. Samples were obtained with informed patient consent and approval from the Research Review Board of the hospital. Cell cultures HCC cell lines (HepG2, Hep3B, MHCC97H, Huh7), were obtained from American Type Culture Collection (ATCC) (Manassas, VA, USA).
