It was also found that HCC patients with high FCGR2A expression had a lower progression-free survival(PFS) than those with low FCGR2A expression ( P < 0.001) ( B, D). FCGR2A is highly expressed in M2 macrophages To validate the above clinical results, we applied experiments to ascertain the expression of FCGR2A in macrophages derived from THP-1. As shown in A, M0 macrophages were obtained from human THP-1 monocytes after being treated with PMA for 24 h. M0 macrophages followed by induction with 50 ng/ml IL-4, 20 ng/ml IL-13 to differentiate M2 macrophages, or 100 ng/ml LPS, 20 ng/ml IFN-γ for 48 h to differentiate into M1 macrophages ( A). M1 and M2 markers were detected by qRT-PCR, the results showed that M1 and M2 were induced successfully ( B). We performed qRT-PCR and Western blot to detect the mRNA and protein levels of FCGR2A in macrophages. qRT-PCR results showed that FCGR2A mRNA was significantly upregulated in M2 macrophages ( C). Western blot results showed that the FCGR2A protein was significantly upregulated in M2 macrophages ( D). FCGR2A induces M2 macrophage polarization via IL-4 The previous results suggested that FCGR2A expressions were significantly upregulated in M2 macrophages, thus we performed more experiments to investigate the function of FCGR2A in M2 polarization. We transfected M0 macrophages with vector or FCGR2A overexpression plasmids. qRT-PCR results showed that M2 markers CD163 and IL10 were significantly upregulated in FCGR2A-overexpressed M0 macrophages ( A). Subsequently, flow cytometry was used to detect the percentage of CD163+ cells in M0 macrophages with transfection of vector or FCGR2A. The results showed that FCGR2A significantly increased the percentage of M2 macrophages ( B). It has been reported that various cytokines are responsible for the polarization of M2 macrophages. Several M2 polarization-associated cytokines were detected by qRT-PCR. The results showed that IL-4 expression was significantly upregulated in macrophages transfected with FCGR2A ( C). Western-blot and ELISA experiments confirmed that protein expression ( D) and secretion levels of IL-4 ( E) were significantly upregulated. What’s more, the addition of IL-4 antibody completely reversed the pro-M2 function of FCGR2A, the addition of IL-4 increased the percentage of M2 macrophages ( F). Taken together, these results demonstrate that FCGR2A induces M2 macrophage polarization via IL-4. FCGR2A exerted its pro-M2 function through IL-4/JAK/STAT6 pathway To determine the downstream target of FCGR2A up-regulated IL-4, we performed Western Blot to detect the JAK/STAT6 pathway in macrophages. JAK/STAT6 pathway has been reported to promote M2 polarization and protect macrophages from senescence [ ]. The results indicated that the phosphorylated levels of JAK1 (JAK1-p) and STAT6 (STAT6-p) were substantially upregulated when M0 macrophages transfected with FCGR2A, while the total levels remained unchanged ( A). Additionally, IL-4 antibodies could markedly suppress the activation of JAK/STAT6 ( A). ELISA assays were employed to measure the levels of IL-10 and IL-13. IL-10 and IL-13 levels were significantly elevated in M0 macrophages transfected with FCGR2A and were reduced upon adding JAK and STAT6 inhibitors

Blot to detect the JAK/STAT6 pathway in macrophages. JAK/STAT6 pathway has been reported to promote M2 polarization and protect macrophages from senescence [ ]. The results indicated that the phosphorylated levels of JAK1 (JAK1-p) and STAT6 (STAT6-p) were substantially upregulated when M0 macrophages transfected with FCGR2A, while the total levels remained unchanged ( A). Additionally, IL-4 antibodies could markedly suppress the activation of JAK/STAT6 ( A). ELISA assays were employed to measure the levels of IL-10 and IL-13. IL-10 and IL-13 levels were significantly elevated in M0 macrophages transfected with FCGR2A and were reduced upon adding JAK and STAT6 inhibitors ( B, C). ELISA results suggested that FCGR2A contributed to M2 polarization through IL-4/JAK/STAT6 pathway. Flow cytometry assays were also utilized to validate the polarization of macrophages. CD163 expression levels in M0 macrophages transfected with FCGR2A decreased upon adding JAK and STAT6 inhibitors ( D). Inhibition of JAK/STAT6 signaling pathway can block the promotion effect of FCGR2A-induced M2 macrophages on HCC cell proliferation We employed inhibitors to suppress the activation of the JAK/STAT6 pathway and detect the influence of macrophages on HCC cell proliferation ( A). The results showed that transfection of FCGR2A in macrophages could significantly promote the proliferation of HepG2 cells ( B). The addition of JAK and STAT6 inhibitors blocked the promotion effect of FCGR2A-induced M2 macrophages on HCC cell proliferation ( B). The results were also confirmed in Hep3B( C), MHCC97L( D), and SK-HEP-1( E). Macrophages with high FCGR2A expression showed an immunosuppressive influence on NK and T cells T cells are the main component of lymphocytes. They possess various biological functions, such as directly killing target cells, assisting or inhibiting B cells in generating antibodies, responding to specific antigens and mitogenic stimuli, and producing cytokines, etc. [ , ]. They are the valiant fighters to resist diseases and infections, as well as tumors [ ]. Different from T and B cells, NK cells are lymphocytes that can kill tumor cells and virus-infected cells without prior sensitization [ ] .We performed co-culture experiments to investigate the role of FCGR2A highly expressed macrophages in regulating T/NK cells functions. We generated stable FCGR2A-overexpressing and vector M2 macrophages and cocultured with NK/T cells. Functional assays included cell viability (CCK8 assays), and cytotoxicity assays (LDH assays) were performed. The results were shown as follows: FCGR2A overexpression macrophages inhibited the cell viability of NK cells ( A), and LDH release experiments showed that M0-FCGR2A inhibited the ability to kill HCC tumor cells of NK cells ( B). What’s more, similar results were obtained in T cells. M0-FCGR2A inhibited the cell viability ( C) and killing activity on HCC tumor cells of T cells ( D). These results showed that macrophages with high FCGR2A expression showed immunosuppressive and tumor-promoting effects. Discussion Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) represents a significant and formidable challenge within China's medical and health domain. Notably, China alone contributes approximately 50 % of the new HCC cases globally [ , ]. The comprehensive treatment regimen for liver cancer commences with tumor resection in the initial stage. Subsequently, several hepatic arterial chemoembolization (TACE) procedures are often carried out. In the later stage, when chemotherapy sensitivity diminishes and recurrence and metastasis occur, targeted drugs and immunotherapy are implemented [ , ]. The occurrence and development of liver cancer will bring huge pain and loss of medical resources to both patients and society [ , ]. Despite the continuous development of existing diagnosis and treatment techniques and the improvement of treatment methods, the possibility of early detection and cure of HCC has greatly increased, but most cases still face adverse outcomes, mainly due to frequent recurrence and metastasis and the formation of drug resistance mechanisms [ ]. The immune-related microenvironment during tumor progression constitutes a complex and intricate ecosystem. It assumes a crucial and indispensable role, spanning from the initiation of cancer to the occurrence of distant metastasis. This renders it a pivotal area of focus in tumor prognosis research [ ]. Macrophages are an important component of the tumor microenvironment, and they are a classic multifunctional immune cell. It can kill tumor cells through innate immune response and act as antigen-presenting cells to activate adaptive immunity and produce anti-tumor effects [ ]. In recent years, the research on the molecular mechanism related to macrophages has become a hot research direction for clinicians. This study was also based on a biogenic analysis of differential expression of related genes in tumor-associated macrophages to screen out genes that may affect the prognosis of liver cancer for clinicopathological verification. Through analysis, we selected FCGR2A as the target gene of this study, and FCGR2A is the gene encoding the FcγRIIa receptor on the surface of macrophages. FCGR2A gene encodes one member of a family of immunoglobulin Fc receptor genes found on the surface of many immune response cells(Immunoglobulin

recent years, the research on the molecular mechanism related to macrophages has become a hot research direction for clinicians. This study was also based on a biogenic analysis of differential expression of related genes in tumor-associated macrophages to screen out genes that may affect the prognosis of liver cancer for clinicopathological verification. Through analysis, we selected FCGR2A as the target gene of this study, and FCGR2A is the gene encoding the FcγRIIa receptor on the surface of macrophages. FCGR2A gene encodes one member of a family of immunoglobulin Fc receptor genes found on the surface of many immune response cells(Immunoglobulin IgG Fc receptor, FcγR) [ , ]. FCGR2A is a cell surface immunoglobulin Fc receptor genes involved in immune response, which play a vital role in immune function and its regulation, and are important participant in many immune system effector functions, such as phagocytosis, the release of inflammatory mediators and antibody-dependent cytotoxicity [ , ]. FCGR2A was widely found in various cancer tissues. In the GEPIA results showed that the expressions of FCGR2A in the carcinoma of the bile duct, carcinoma of the esophagus, cystadenocarcinoma,the clear cell carcinoma of the kidney, the glioblastoma multiforme,HNSC, renal papillary,cell carcinoma, low-grade cerebral glioma, ovary serous, carcinoma of the pancreas, melanoma, and gastric cancer tissues were significantly higher than that of the corresponding adjacent tissues. In contrast, the expressions of FCGR2A in the diffuse large B cell lymphoma, adrenocortical carcinoma, pulmonary squamous carcinoma, acute myeloid leukemia, and thymus cancer tissues were significantly lower than that of the corresponding adjacent tissues [ ]. FCGR2A was upregulated in ccRCC patients compared to normal renal tissue. The patients with high expression of FCGR2A had poor OS [ ]. FCGR2A expression in several carcinoma tissues was significantly higher than in adjacent tissues. FCGR2A could function as a prognostic marker and correlate with immune infiltration in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma [ ]. FCGR2A knockdown suppresses M1 macrophage polarization and NF- κ B phosphorylation while enhancing M2 polarization and STAT3 activation, leading to ameliorated IDD in animal models [ ]. Up to now, there are few studies focusing on the expression of FCGR2A in macrophages among HCC patients. In our study, it was noted that FCGR2A was differentially expressed between cancer tissues and para-cancer tissues of patients with hepatocellular carcinoma. The expression level of FCGR2A was significantly increased in patients with extrahepatic metastasis, larger tumor diameters, postoperative pathological specimens, and positive satellite nodules. Immunofluorescence and immunohistochemical staining results showed that the expression level of FCGR2A in cancer tissues was higher than that in adjacent tissues, and FCGR2A mainly exists in M2 macrophages in cancer tissues. Kaplan-Meier analysis showed that HCC patients with high expression of FCGR2A had poor survival prognosis. In vivo experiments showed that FCGR2A was significantly upregulated in M2 macrophages. Transfection of FCGR2A could promote the polarization of M0 macrophages into M2.qRT-PCR and western blot results showed that FCGR2A activated JAK/STAT6 pathway by upregulating IL-4. Inhibition of JAK/STAT6 signaling pathway can block the promotion effect of FCGR2A-induced M2 macrophages on HCC cell proliferation. Our research still has some limitations. We need in vivo validation using immunocompetent HCC models. The interactions between macrophages and NK/T cells also needs more investigation. Challenges include interpatient variability in macrophage polarization states, and potential redundancy in immune regulatory pathways [ ]. To address these, we will collaborate with pharmacologists to optimize inhibitor specificity and design multi-omic correlative studies in patient-derived macrophages and chemically-induced HCC model of transgenic mice with macrophage-specific high expression of FCGR2A. We will employ immunohistochemistry, flow cytometry, and spatial transcriptomics to map alterations in immune cell composition, activation status (such as IFN-γ+ T cells, granzyme B + NK cells) in future work. Single-cell RNA sequencing will further dissect the transcriptional signatures of T/NK cells and macrophages, enabling us to identify synergistic or antagonistic interactions modulated by FCGR2A inhibition. We acknowledge that spatial and single-cell resolution (e.g., multiplex IHC, CyTOF) in treated models will be required to fully validate these interactions. Additionally, we will outline a roadmap for preclinical optimization (dose-ranging studies, combination sequencing) and future clinical trial design. Conclusion FCGR2A is highly expressed in M2 macrophages in liver cancer tissues. The expression level of FCGR2A is found to be associated with extrahepatic metastasis, maximum tumor diameter, CNLC stage, satellite nodule, and differentiation degree. High FCGR2A expression predicts lower OS and PFS in HCC patients. Subsequent experiments showed that FCGR2A promoted polarization of M2 macrophages by activating the IL-4/JAK/STAT6 pathway. What’s more, macrophages with high FCGR2A expression showed an immunosuppressive influence on NK and T cells viabilities and killing activities. Inhibition of JAK/STAT6 signaling pathway is capable of impeding the promoting effect of FCGR2A-induced M2 macrophages on HCC cell proliferation. documents.title: AASLD Practice Guidance on Acute on Chronic Liver Failure

chunks.content: Introduction Acute-on-chronic liver failure (ACLF) is a severe clinical syndrome characterized by acute hepatic decompensation, extrahepatic organ damage, and high short-term mortality, [ , ] which occurs on the basis of chronic liver diseases. The concept of ACLF was first proposed by Ohnishi et al [ ] in 1995, to describe two simultaneous lesions or insults to the liver, namely, an acute and rapid deterioration in liver function in individuals with preexisting chronic liver disease that was characterized by decompensated liver failure, high incidence of organ failure, and extremely high short-term mortality. In the nearly 30 years since the concept was proposed, it has been widely accepted by scholars all over the world. However, there is still no unified standard clinical definition for the diagnosis of ACLF worldwide. To better understand ACLF, the continuous comprehension and development of the clinical definition of ACLF is reviewed in this study. Furthermore, we have consolidated the current understanding of ACLF pathogenesis and summarized the therapeutic targets for ACLF that are currently under investigation. Last, we propose an experimental mouse model that can contribute to the mechanistic understanding of ACLF and the evaluation of potential new therapies. Disease Definition of ACLF Since the concept of ACLF was first proposed in 1995, its definition has been a subject of ongoing debate for nearly 30 years. Nevertheless, with the advancement of large-scale, well-characterized ACLF cohort studies conducted by different organizations and institutions, the definition of ACLF has progressively been clarified and refined. In 2006, the Chinese Society of Infectious Diseases and the Chinese Society of Hepatology of the Chinese Medical Association (CMA) described ACLF as: acute decompensation of liver function on the basis of chronic liver diseases. [ ] In 2009, the ACLF working group of Asian-Pacific Association for the Study of the Liver (APASL) published the first expert consensus on ACLF for the Asia-Pacific region. ACLF was defined as: acute deterioration of liver function manifested by jaundice (total bilirubin [TBil] ≥5 mg/dL or ≥85.5 μmol/L) and coagulopathy (international normalized ratio [INR] ≥1.5 or prothrombin activity [PTA] <40%), and complicated clinical ascites and/or encephalopathy within 4 weeks, regardless of whether the patient has previously diagnosed or undiagnosed chronic liver disease (including cirrhosis). [ ] In 2012, the CMA released the “Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Treatment of Liver Failure (2012 Edition)”, which also updated the definition of ACLF, pointing out that ACLF is a clinical syndrome of acute or subacute decompensation of liver function that occurs within a short period, usually within 4 weeks, on the basis of chronic liver diseases. [ ] Also in 2012, the APASL–ACLF Research Consortium (AARC) was formed to collect prospective data of patients with ACLF. [ ] In 2013, based on the results of a prospective multicenter study (Consortium for the Development of Criteria for Acute-on-Chronic Liver Failure [CANONIC]) involving 1343 patients from eight European countries, the Chronic Liver Failure Consortium (CLIF-C) of the European Association for the Study of the Liver (EASL) described ACLF as an acute deterioration of liver cirrhosis, usually correlating with a preceding disease characterized by organ failure and high short-term mortality (28-day mortality ≥15%). [ ] They proposed the CLIF–sequential organ failure assessment (SOFA) score to define ACLF and used SOFA score to diagnose organ failures. [ , ] According to the number of organ failures, ACLF is divided into three different grades (ACLF grades 1, 2, and 3), with 28‑day mortality rates of 22%, 32%, and 76% and 90‑day mortality rates of 40%, 52%, and 79%, respectively. The EASL–CLIF ACLF score (or CLIF–C ACLF score) does not reflect the severity of liver failure itself but provides useful information for predicting mortality and transplant inefficiency in Western patients with ACLF. In July 2014, the North American Consortium for the Study of End-stage Liver Disease (NACSELD) observed the outcomes of 507 hospitalized patients with decompensated cirrhosis caused by alcohol or hepatitis C and complicated with infection from 18 centers of liver diseases in the United States and Canada. They proposed the concept of infection-related ACLF (I-ACLF), which was defined as acute deterioration of a patient with cirrhosis due to infection presenting with two or more extrahepatic organ failure, such as grade III or IV hepatic encephalopathy, circulatory shock, need for mechanical ventilation, dialysis or other forms of renal replacement therapy, with high short-term mortality. [ ] This disease definition does not include changes in liver function and coagulation function. In October 2014, APASL updated the expert consensus based on the prospective study cohort data (AARC data) from the Asia–Pacific region. The cohort was constituted with 1363 patients from 14 countries. The updated definition of ACLF adopted some of the concepts of EASL–CLIF–C, and the characteristic of “high short-term (28-day) mortality” was added. [ ] Also in 2014, to bridge the gap between the disease definitions of

In October 2014, APASL updated the expert consensus based on the prospective study cohort data (AARC data) from the Asia–Pacific region. The cohort was constituted with 1363 patients from 14 countries. The updated definition of ACLF adopted some of the concepts of EASL–CLIF–C, and the characteristic of “high short-term (28-day) mortality” was added. [ ] Also in 2014, to bridge the gap between the disease definitions of ACLF from different agencies in the East and the West, the World Gastroenterology Organisation (WGO) proposed a new consensus, integrating existing concepts and ideas, defining ACLF as a syndrome that occurs in patients with chronic liver diseases with or without cirrhosis, characterized by acute liver failure (ALF) (jaundice and INR prolongation) caused by acute liver decompensation, single or multiple extrahepatic organ failures, resulting in an increased mortality rate within 3 months. In addition, ACLF was divided into three types: (1) type A, ACLF without cirrhosis; (2) type B, ACLF with compensated cirrhosis; and (3) type C, ACLF with decompensated cirrhosis. [ ] In 2018, the “Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Treatment of Liver Failure (2018 Edition)” of the CMA was updated, further improving the definition of ACLF as: on the basis of chronic liver diseases, a syndrome characterized by acute jaundice deepening and coagulation dysfunction as manifestations of liver failure caused by various precipitating factors, which may be combined with complications such as hepatic encephalopathy, ascites, electrolyte disorders, infections, hepatorenal syndrome, and hepatopulmonary syndrome, as well as other extrahepatic organ failure. [ ] At the same time, the update in this guideline also included the different ACLF types as proposed by the WGO, dividing ACLF into three types: (1) type A, ACLF occurring on the basis of chronic noncirrhotic liver diseases; (2) type B, ACLF occurring on the basis of compensated cirrhosis, usually within 4 weeks; and (3) type C, ACLF occurring on the basis of decompensated cirrhosis. In 2018, through the establishment of Chinese Group on the Study of Severe Hepatitis B (COSSH), Chinese scholars completed a study involving 1322 hospitalized patients with acute decompensation of hepatitis B cirrhosis or acute injury of chronic hepatitis B from 13 centers of liver diseases. Considering the fact that the clinical characteristics of hepatitis B virus infection-related ACLF (HBV–ACLF) in the East are different from those of alcoholic liver disease-related ACLF (ALD–ACLF) in the West, they summarized the clinical characteristics of HBV–ACLF in the East and defined HBV–ACLF as: in patients with chronic liver disease due to HBV infection, acute decompensation with liver or extrahepatic organ failure is associated with high short-term mortality. When TBil ≥12 mg/dL and prothrombin time (PT)–INR ≥1.5, ACLF should be diagnosed. This approach refines the HBV-related ACLF definition, filling the gap in EASL–ACLF criteria, which are not fully applicable to patients with hepatitis B in China. [ ] In 2019, based on the prospective multicenter study cohort data of 5228 patients from 43 centers in 15 countries in the Asia–Pacific region, the APASL–AARC once again updated the APASL consensus on ACLF, adding the description that “ACLF is a reversible syndrome” to the original disease definition, taking the reversibility of the disease as an important feature of ACLF, and pointing out that this reversibility is manifested as the decrease of TBil and PT–INR, as well as the improvement of hepatic encephalopathy or ascites. [ ] In 2022, the American College of Gastroenterology (ACG) released the “Clinical Guidelines for Acute-on-Chronic Liver Failure” for the first time based on the three international ACLF guidelines launched by APASL, EASL, and NACSELD, pointing out that ACLF is a potentially reversible disease that occurs in patients with chronic liver diseases with or without cirrhosis, and may lead to multiorgan failure and death within 3 months in the absence of basic treatment for liver disease, liver support treatment, or liver transplantation. ACLF is identified by chronic liver diseases, elevated serum TBil, and prolonged INR, and the occurrence of kidney, respiratory, circulatory, or brain function failure during the course of the disease, which is a further basis for ACLF diagnosis. The disease description of ACLF by the ACG is similar to the definitions of the CMA and APASL guidelines, and emphasizes more on the reversibility of the disease. In April 2023, the EASL once again updated the clinical practice guidelines for ACLF, evaluating and comparing the disease definitions and standards of ACLF proposed by APSAL, NACSELD, and COSSH, pointing out the deficiencies in APSAL and NACSELD, and emphasizing that the update of this guideline aims to help clinicians identify ACLF, rationally allocate treatment resources, and develop management strategies. In April 2023, the EASL once again updated the clinical practice guidelines for ACLF, evaluating and comparing the disease definitions and standards of ACLF proposed by APSAL, NACSELD, and COSSH, pointing out the deficiencies in APSAL and NACSELD, and emphasizing that the update of this guideline aims to help clinicians identify ACLF, rationally allocate treatment resources, and develop management strategies. The disease definition of ACLF described in this version of the guideline is adjusted and improved from the 2013 version to: ACLF is a severe form of acute decompensation of cirrhosis, associated with a high 28-day mortality rate (≥20%), manifested as the failure of one up to six organ system (including the liver, kidney, brain, coagulation, circulation, and respiration), and the onset of acute factors that lead to systemic inflammation (SI), including intrahepatic and/or extrahepatic damage. [ ] In June 2023, during the 12th National Conference of the China Network for Severe Liver Diseases (CNSLD) held in Dalian, China, we proposed that ACLF could be divided into two types, based on the characteristics of intrahepatic and extrahepatic organ failures at the onset of ACLF [Figure ]. [ ] Type I ACLF: liver failure without extrahepatic organ failures Acute liver injury on the basis of chronic liver diseases, mainly manifested as jaundice and coagulation dysfunction. At the onset of ACLF, the affected organ is the liver, and some patients have hepatic encephalopathy. Liver failure is the first manifestation, and other organ failures do not occur simultaneously, and the disease definition is close to the content of APASL and CMA. [ , ] Type II ACLF: liver failure with extrahepatic organ failures Mostly acute decompensation of liver function on the basis of cirrhosis, manifested as elevated TBil, prolonged PT–INR, and the occurrence of complications of cirrhosis, accompanied by liver and at least one extrahepatic organ failure within 1 week, and the disease definition is close to the content of EASL–CLIF, COSSH, and NACSELD. [ , ] This classification and disease definition are of positive significance for bridging the gap between different associations in the East and the West regarding ACLF. However, it is worth further carrying out prospective multicenter studies to expand and confirm this classification and disease definition. In November 2023, the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases (AASLD) released a practice guideline proposing that any definition of ACLF needs to include the presence of hepatic dysfunction as well as the presence of extrahepatic organ failure. They recognized ACLF as multiorgan failure in patients with chronic liver disease, emphasizing its reversibility and the role of liver transplantation and supportive care. [ ] In March 2024, similar classification for ACLF (types A and B) was proposed in India. [ ] Moreover, at the APASL annual meeting held in Kyoto in March 2024, the “Kyoto APASL Consensus” proposed a unified ACLF definition based on the two-type classification (types A and B) and further refined the specific content of this definition. Type A ACLF excludes patients with earlier decompensation or those experiencing extrahepatic organ injury, and its course is considered reversible. Type B ACLF is defined similarly to the COSSH definition of ACLF and may include patients with earlier decompensation and organ failure caused by intra- or extrahepatic injuries (including infections), which is associated with increased mortality. Type A ACLF encompasses definitions from APASL and Japanese definitions, while Type B ACLF corresponds to the AASLD, EASL–CLIF, NACSELD, and COSSH definitions. Type A ACLF can be further stratified into grades A1, A2, and A3 based on the AARC score. ACLF defined by NACSELD can be reclassified into B2 and B3 based on the number of organ failures. [ ] This has made certain contributions to unifying the definitions of ACLF between the East and the West. In December 2024, the CMA released the “Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Treatment of Liver Failure (2024 Edition)”, incorporating key concepts from the COSSH standards. [ ] In April 2025, the Chinese Society of Hepatology of CMA released the first “Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Treatment of Acute-on-Chronic Liver Failure (ACLF) (2025 Edition)” in China, which builds upon the content related to ACLF from the “Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Treatment of Liver Failure (2024 Edition)”. It systematically classifies ACLF into type I (liver failure without extrahepatic organ failure) and type II (liver failure with extrahepatic organ failure) for separate description in clinical practice. [ ] By sorting out the descriptions for the disease definition of ACLF by various societies or organizations in recent years, we can clearly recognize the research progress that has been made in the field of ACLF [Table ]. The

and Treatment of Acute-on-Chronic Liver Failure (ACLF) (2025 Edition)” in China, which builds upon the content related to ACLF from the “Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Treatment of Liver Failure (2024 Edition)”. It systematically classifies ACLF into type I (liver failure without extrahepatic organ failure) and type II (liver failure with extrahepatic organ failure) for separate description in clinical practice. [ ] By sorting out the descriptions for the disease definition of ACLF by various societies or organizations in recent years, we can clearly recognize the research progress that has been made in the field of ACLF [Table ]. The APASL definition is simple and easy to use, emphasizing liver failure itself, which aligns with the epidemiological trend in the Asia–Pacific region, where viral hepatitis is predominant. This definition facilitates early diagnosis and treatment of ACLF, helping prevent progression to multiorgan failure. However, it pays insufficient attention to other organ failures and is not suitable for patients outside the Asia–Pacific region. Compared to the APASL definition, the EASL–ACLF includes patients with decompensated cirrhosis in its definition, emphasizing multiorgan failure and SI. It is more comprehensive and suitable for patients with multiorgan failure in Europe, particularly in cases requiring a holistic assessment of prognosis. However, it is not applicable to noncirrhotic patients. Additionally, NACSELD focuses on defining infection-related ACLF, making it particularly suitable for populations in North America where infections are prevalent, especially in cases of infection-induced multiorgan failure. Nevertheless, it is limited to infection-related ACLF, narrowing its scope of application, and does not emphasize liver failure itself. [ ] Although scholars around the world still have some different understanding of ACLF, the global research on ACLF is indeed gradually deepening and the understanding of ACLF is gradually improving. Thereby, a consensus for a general description of the disease definition of ACLF is gradually approaching. ACLF is different from ALF and chronic liver failure (CLF) and has unique clinical characteristics and prognostic outcomes. Therefore, establishing a clear disease definition of ACLF is of great significance for the early detection, diagnosis, and treatment of ACLF. With a deeper understanding of ACLF, global multicenter large-sample cohort studies are warranted to reach a general consensus on the definition of ACLF. Current Understanding of the Pathogenesis of ACLF In China and the Asia–Pacific region, the basic chronic liver disease in ACLF is mainly chronic hepatitis B, while in European and American countries, it is mainly alcoholic hepatitis and chronic hepatitis C. [ ] Although there are differences in the underlying liver diseases between the East and the West, the common pathological basis of most patients with ACLF is usually liver fibrosis or cirrhosis caused by long-term chronic liver injury. [ ] After suffering from acute intrahepatic or extrahepatic injury, acute decompensation of liver function occurs, such as jaundice, coagulation dysfunction, hepatic encephalopathy, and ascites, and eventually progresses to systemic multiorgan failure. [ ] At present, it is generally believed that the systemic inflammatory response induced by acute liver injury and bacterial infection, on the basis of long-term chronic liver injury, plays an important role in the outcome of ACLF. [ ] A large amount of clinical data also shows that the high short-term mortality of patients with ACLF is related to bacterial infection. [ ] In a multicenter ACLF cohort study of 407 patients, the EASL–CLIF research group found through that 37% of patients had bacterial infection at admission, and 46% of the remaining patients without infection at admission developed bacterial infection within 4 weeks of follow-up, mainly spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, urinary tract infection, and pneumonia, suggesting that bacterial infection is widespread in patients with ACLF (>66%) and directly affects the clinical outcome. [ ] Alcohol-associated hepatitis is a major form of ACLF in Western countries, [ ] neutrophils are well known to play an important role in the pathogenesis of alcohol-associated hepatitis. [ ] A recent study demonstrated that the self-sustaining interleukin 8 (IL-8 + ) neutrophils are the major driver to promote alcohol-associated hepatitis disease progression and liver failure, [ ] which are potential therapeutic targets for alcohol-associated hepatitis. [ ] It would be interesting to determine whether IL-8 + neutrophils also play an important role in the pathogenesis of ACLF induced by other etiologies, such as HBV and HCV. In 2016, based on the CANONIC cohort, the EASL–CLIF research group proposed the well-known “SI hypothesis”, believing that ACLF is an acute exacerbation of the existing SI in patients with decompensated cirrhosis. [ ] The research group evaluated the systemic inflammatory response by detecting the levels of 29 cytokines in the serum of 522 patients with decompensated cirrhosis (237 patients with ACLF) and 40 healthy controls. They clinically confirmed the SI hypothesis and found that SI is the primary driving force for the progression of ACLF in patients with cirrhosis. [ ] In

[ ] The research group evaluated the systemic inflammatory response by detecting the levels of 29 cytokines in the serum of 522 patients with decompensated cirrhosis (237 patients with ACLF) and 40 healthy controls. They clinically confirmed the SI hypothesis and found that SI is the primary driving force for the progression of ACLF in patients with cirrhosis. [ ] In May 2020, renowned experts in the field of ACLF systematically concluded the definition, clinical features, pathophysiology, and prevention and treatment principles of ACLF caused by cirrhosis. They further pointed out that although the pathogenesis of ACLF is not entirely clear currently, systemic inflammatory response plays an important role in the course of ACLF. [ ] In patients with cirrhosis, the massive release of pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) and damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) activates immune cells by binding to specific pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) of innate immune cells, leading to excessive systemic inflammatory response, causing immune-mediated tissue damage, and then causing single or multiple organ damage, and finally progressing to ACLF. [ ] Severe SI can lead to insufficient tissue perfusion, immune-mediated tissue damage, and mitochondrial dysfunction. [ , ] Among them, mitochondrial dysfunction is related to the progression of ACLF. In patients with ACLF, oxidative phosphorylation and adenosine triphosphate (ATP) production are reduced, which may aggravate organ failure. Excessive release of proinflammatory cytokines consumes a large amount of energy. Coupled with the obstruction of energy production, it will eventually lead to immune exhaustion/immune paralysis. [ ] This immune dysfunction will increase the risk of secondary infection and lead to a higher mortality rate. [ ] In March 2021, core members of the EASL–CLIF research group again emphasized that the SI hypothesis is a new paradigm of acute decompensation and multiorgan failure in cirrhosis. [ ] Dr. Didier Samuel wrote an Editorial in the same issue and commented on the SI hypothesis proposed by Arroyo et al [ ] , pointing out that this hypothesis has introduced two new concepts in the field of ACLF: (1) Systemic inflammatory response is the driving factor for the development of decompensation in cirrhosis and (2) the increased incidence of bacterial infections in patients with cirrhosis is also the result of immune exhaustion or immune paralysis after systemic inflammatory response. [ ] It was further pointed out that with the elucidation of the mechanism of systemic inflammatory response in ACLF, it will lead to the application of anti-inflammatory therapies in the field of ACLF, and he also indicated that more work should be done to determine whether SI and immunoparesis are drivers or complications of decompensated cirrhosis. [ ] In conclusion, the pathogenesis of ACLF is comprehensive and complex, yet remains not fully elucidated. It is typically explained by the PIRO concept, including predisposition (P), injury (I), response (R), and organ failure (O). ACLF develops on the basis of long-term chronic liver damage caused by an underlying liver disease (predisposition). Following the sustention of various acute intrahepatic or extrahepatic injuries (injury), patients initially present with acute decompensation of liver function. This condition manifests as hyperbilirubinemia, coagulation disorders, hepatic encephalopathy, and ascites. The immune system response (response) induced by this injury can be divided into two aspects. One aspect is that, following acute liver injury, the cellular immunity and the reticuloendothelial cell system in the liver become imbalanced, and the ability of the liver to synthesize various anti-infectious proteins decreases, increasing the risk of bacterial infections (e.g., spontaneous bacterial peritonitis caused by intestinal flora translocation, urinary tract infections, pneumonia, and skin and soft tissue infections). Bacterial infections will lead to the presence of a large number of PAMPs in patients’ circulation. The other aspect is that necrotic hepatocytes release a large number of DAMPs into the systemic circulation. Circulating DAMPs and PAMPs bind to specific PRRs of innate immune cells, thereby activating the immune system. This activation then triggers the release of numerous proinflammatory cytokines, including tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNF-α), IL-1β, IL-2, IL-4, IL-6, IL-8, IL-10, IL-17, and interferon gamma (IFN-γ), which results in SI and a cytokine storm. This will stimulate a systemic inflammatory response that leads to subsequent immune-mediated tissue damage. After patients experience excessive systemic inflammatory response in the early stage of the ACLF, the late stage of the disease progresses to a state of immune exhaustion or immune paralysis, with bacterial infections further aggravated. Meanwhile, single or multiple organ dysfunction may occur. Subsequently, patients may progress to liver failure either without or with extrahepatic organ failure (Organ failure). Eventually, ACLF progresses to multiple organ failure, ultimately leading to the death of

IL-10, IL-17, and interferon gamma (IFN-γ), which results in SI and a cytokine storm. This will stimulate a systemic inflammatory response that leads to subsequent immune-mediated tissue damage. After patients experience excessive systemic inflammatory response in the early stage of the ACLF, the late stage of the disease progresses to a state of immune exhaustion or immune paralysis, with bacterial infections further aggravated. Meanwhile, single or multiple organ dysfunction may occur. Subsequently, patients may progress to liver failure either without or with extrahepatic organ failure (Organ failure). Eventually, ACLF progresses to multiple organ failure, ultimately leading to the death of the patient [Figure ]. [ ] Three-stage ACLF Mouse Model and Pathogenesis Progress At present, the existing experimental animal models for ACLF can be classified into three major categories: (1) hepatotoxic reagent-induced ACLF, (2) immune response-induced ACLF, and (3) surgical procedure-induced ACLF models. These models are designed to simulate different aspects of the disease pathogenesis by combining various induction methods. The principles, protocols, advantages, and disadvantages of these experimental models for ACLF are summarized in Table . In brief, hepatotoxic reagent-induced ACLF models include protocols using carbon tetrachloride (CCl 4 ), thioacetamide (TAA), and acetaminophen (APAP) to induce chronic liver injury followed by acute insults, such as D-galactosamine (D-GalN) and lipopolysaccharide (LPS). These models are widely used for studying liver fibrosis and acute injury. These models tend to have high mortality rates and short survival time, especially after the acute insult. Immune response-induced ACLF models primarily focus on immune responses by using substances, such as human serum albumin (HSA) and porcine serum (PS) for chronic injury, followed by D-GalN and LPS for acute injury. These models are particularly useful for studying autoimmune or viral hepatitis-related ACLF. While they provide valuable insights into immune-driven ACLF, they lack direct hepatotoxicity modeling and have high variability in immune responses. Surgical procedure-induced ACLF models include protocols such as bile duct ligation (BDL) with LPS, or BDL combined with hepatic ischemia/reperfusion injury. These models are suitable for studying cholestatic liver diseases and ischemic hepatitis. However, they require advanced surgical skills and have high mortality rates due to infection or complications from surgery. However, none of the existing ACLF models, whether induced by hepatotoxic reagents, immune responses, or surgical procedures, could fully replicate the entire disease course seen in patients with ACLF, making them imperfect representations of the condition. Based on the clinical characteristics of patients with ACLF, the optimal experimental animal model should be able to simulate the core pathological features of ACLF, including chronic liver injury, acute exacerbation, and multiorgan failure. Moreover, the reagents used for modeling should be easily accessible, and the induction methods should be simple and straightforward. Additionally, the model should allow for a reasonable survival period, ideally around one week, to facilitate intervention studies and better assess therapeutic efficacy. Due to the lack of optimal experimental animal models for ACLF, the progress of basic investigation of ACLF is limping. Although several experimental ACLF models have been established, none of them can recapitulate and simulate the whole pathological process of patients with ACLF. [ , ] Current research on the mechanisms of ACLF suggests that bacterial infection and systemic inflammatory response are crucial in the progression of the disease. [ , ] Based on cohort studies in patients with ACLF, it was found that the key clinical courses of most patients with ACLF can be divided into three stages: (1) long-term chronic liver injury, (2) acute liver injury, and (3) bacterial infection and systemic inflammatory response with extrahepatic organ damage. Recently, according to these three stages, our group has designed and developed a three-stage ACLF mouse model combining chronic liver injury, induced by injection of CCl 4 for 8 weeks, acute hepatic insult, obtained by injection of a double dose of CCl 4 , and bacterial infection caused through intraperitoneal injection of Klebsiella pneumoniae [Figure ]. [ , ] Using this mouse model, we were able to successfully simulat the key courses and major clinical features of patients with ACLF. Moreover, this model can also well simulate the extrahepatic organ damage that occurs during the progression of the disease, including acute kidney injury and multiple organ failure. It has an appropriate survival period for intervention research and provides a reliable tool for mechanistic investigation of ACLF. [ , ] The three-stage ACLF mouse model provides a comprehensive simulation of the key clinical features of ACLF, including chronic liver injury, acute insults, bacterial infection, and multiorgan injury. It is particularly useful for therapeutic research due to its ability to mimic the pathophysiological progression of ACLF, offering a survival window of 5–7 days suitable for preclinical intervention studies. The inclusion of viable bacterial infections, a critical feature in ACLF, further enhances its relevance. [ , ] Using the three-stage ACLF mouse model, our

It is particularly useful for therapeutic research due to its ability to mimic the pathophysiological progression of ACLF, offering a survival window of 5–7 days suitable for preclinical intervention studies. The inclusion of viable bacterial infections, a critical feature in ACLF, further enhances its relevance. [ , ] Using the three-stage ACLF mouse model, our group found that the imbalance of signal transducer and activator of transcription 1 (STAT1)/STAT3 activation in the liver affecting liver regeneration is an important mechanism for the continuous progression of ACLF. It is mainly affected by excessive expression of IFN-γ and bacterial infection. Liver tissue and peripheral blood of patients with HBV–ACLF and ALD–ACLF confirmed that liver regeneration was significantly inhibited during the systemic inflammatory response. By regulating the imbalance of STAT1/STAT3 activation in the liver in the ACLF mouse model, the mortality rate of ACLF mice can be improved. Subsequently, it was found that the innate immune-related cytokine interleukin-22 (IL-22) can reverse the imbalance of STAT1/STAT3 activation in the liver and promote liver regeneration, thereby blocking the disease progression in ACLF mice. [ , ] Based on this study, a multicenter phase II clinical trial on treating ACLF with IL-22 fusion protein (IL-22Fc, F-652) is currently underway. At present, most studies on the mechanism of ACLF are related to systemic inflammatory response and immune dysfunction. Zhang et al [ ] found that the expression of V-domain Ig suppressor of T-cell activation (VISTA) in peripheral blood and liver tissue of patients with ACLF was significantly reduced. The excessive differentiation of Th17 cells and the massive release of proinflammatory cytokines were related to the downregulation of VISTA expression. Using the three-stage ACLF model, activating VISTA expression in ACLF mice can inhibit the activation of CD4 + T cells, reduce inflammation, and reduce mortality. He et al [ ] found through transcriptomic studies that the expression of transcription factor ETS Proto-Oncogene 2 (ETS2) in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) of patients with ACLF was significantly higher than that in patients with chronic liver disease and healthy control. Moreover, ETS2 can be used to predict the 28/90-day mortality rate of patients with ACLF. It was confirmed that ETS2 has the effect of inhibiting excessive inflammatory response in mice model. Bernsmeier et al [ ] found that the expression of MER receptor tyrosine kinase (MERTK) was upregulated in patients with ACLF. MERTK is mainly expressed on monocytes–macrophages and inhibits innate immune responses. The number of monocytes–macrophages with high expression of MERTK in patients with ACLF increased significantly, inhibiting innate immune responses and increasing the risk of bacterial infection in patients with ACLF. Bernsmeier et al [ ] also found that CD14 + CD15-HLA-DR-myeloid-derived suppressor cells (M-MDSCs) were significantly increased in patients with ACLF. This type of cell can inhibit T-cell function and weaken the antimicrobial innate immune response. It is related to secondary infection, disease severity, and prognosis of patients with ACLF. Yao et al [ ] detected the situation of T cells in the peripheral blood of patients with HBV–ACLF by single-cell sequencing technology and found that peripheral blood T cells in patients with ACLF are diverse, including naive T cells, effector T cells, and exhausted T cells. The frequency of exhausted T cells in patients with ACLF increased significantly during the progression of ACLF, suggesting that T-cell exhaustion promotes the occurrence of immune dysfunction (immune exhaustion/immune paralysis) in patients with ACLF. Peng et al [ ] used single-cell RNA sequencing to analyze liver nonparenchymal cells (NPCs) and PBMCs from healthy controls, and patients with liver cirrhosis and ACLF. They also examined a series of inflammation-related cytokines and chemokines in liver and plasma samples, as well as the lipid metabolome targeting free-fatty acids in the liver. The results revealed macrophage reprogramming in the liver during ACLF. Immunosuppressive triggering receptor expressed on myeloid cells 2 (TREM2) + macrophages were enriched in ACLF livers and contributed to an immunosuppressive hepatic microenvironment. The accumulation of unsaturated fatty acids in ACLF livers promoted macrophage reprogramming, highlighting the regulation of lipid metabolism as a potential target for improving immune dysfunction in patients with ACLF. [ ] Yang et al [ ] found that semaphorin-6B (SEMA6B) is significantly overexpressed in HBV-related patients with ACLF compared to healthy individuals. It mediates SI by inducing macrophages and inhibits proliferation through G0/G1 cell cycle arrest, thereby promoting hepatocyte apoptosis. These findings highlight SEMA6B as a promising early therapeutic target for patients with HBV–ACLF. [ ] Yu et al [ ] found that the levels of B- and T-lymphocyte attenuator (BTLA) were significantly

[ ] Yang et al [ ] found that semaphorin-6B (SEMA6B) is significantly overexpressed in HBV-related patients with ACLF compared to healthy individuals. It mediates SI by inducing macrophages and inhibits proliferation through G0/G1 cell cycle arrest, thereby promoting hepatocyte apoptosis. These findings highlight SEMA6B as a promising early therapeutic target for patients with HBV–ACLF. [ ] Yu et al [ ] found that the levels of B- and T-lymphocyte attenuator (BTLA) were significantly increased in circulating and intrahepatic CD4 + T cells in patients with HBV–ACLF, which were positively correlated with disease severity, prognosis, and infection complications. Using the three-stage ACLF mice model, BTLA knockdown or administration of anti-BTLA antibody indicated increased cytokine secretion, reduced mortality and bacterial burden, showing a potential therapeutic target. [ ] Therapeutic Strategies and New Advances Currently, there is no specific and effective treatment for ACLF, the core principles of managing ACLF revolve around organ support and targeted interventions. [ ] Organ support aims to stabilize critical functions such as the liver, kidneys, and circulatory system, while targeted interventions focus on addressing specific triggers, such as infections or SI. Early identification and treatment of these triggers are crucial for improving patient outcomes. Traditional treatment concepts for ACLF mainly include etiological treatment, supportive and symptomatic treatments, artificial liver support systems, and liver transplantation. The precise triggering factors of ACLF remain elusive; however, in 40%–50% of ACLF cases, bacterial translocation linked to SI is regarded as a critical determinant. When the trigger is identified, early recognition and targeted intervention of the causative factor would significantly improve the prognosis of patients with ACLF. However, a significant proportion of patients exhibit no identifiable triggering factors, substantially complicating the treatment process. [ ] Bacterial infection represents the most common trigger in patients with ACLF, exacerbating the disease course and significantly worsening the prognosis. A recent study revealed that approximately 37% of patients with ACLF presented with bacterial infections at the time of diagnosis. An additional 46% of patients developed bacterial infections within the subsequent 4 weeks. [ ] Regardless of the severity of ACLF, the prognosis of infected patients is significantly poorer compared to that of uninfected patients. [ ] Therefore, systematic pathogen detection and antimicrobial susceptibility testing should be performed upon hospital admission. Empirical antibiotic therapy should be initiated promptly upon the appearance of infection signs and subsequently adjusted based on pathogen detection and susceptibility results. [ ] For patients without infections, recent studies indicate that prophylactic use of antibiotics may reduce the risk of infection during the ACLF course, thereby decreasing mortality rates. [ , ] HBV reactivation is one of the most common triggers of ACLF in Asian countries and is associated with a high short-term mortality rate. [ ] Therefore, once HBV reactivation is suspected, immediate initiation of antiviral therapy with oral nucleotide or nucleoside analogues is recommended. For patients with ACLF and alcoholic liver disease, alcohol abstinence and corticosteroids remain the first-line therapeutic strategy. [ ] Artificial liver support system (ALSS) is a critical component of the comprehensive medical treatment of ACLF and serves as an essential bridging therapy for patients awaiting liver transplantation. [ ] These modalities include plasma exchange, blood/plasma adsorption, hemofiltration, hemodialysis, and various integrated blood purification systems. Extracorporeal liver support systems can rapidly improve the body’s internal environment and overall condition, mitigating further damage to the liver or other organs, while creating conditions for liver regeneration and recovery. In ACLF, liver cell injury is predominantly driven by cytokine storms and toxin accumulation. [ ] ALSS could effectively remove toxins produced during liver failure and reduce the levels of proinflammatory cytokines such as TNF-α and IL-6. Additionally, it also ameliorates cholestasis, enhances liver and renal function, and stabilizes hemodynamics, thereby providing patients with ACLF and improved survival opportunities or a better chance to await liver transplantation. [ ] Compared to conventional drug therapy, ALSS has been shown to significantly reduce the mortality rates in HBV–ACLF. [ ] However, according to the latest EASL clinical guidelines, extracorporeal liver support therapies, whether artificial or biological, are not routinely recommended for ACLF outside of research trials. [ ] Liver transplantation is one of the most effective approaches for managing end-stage liver failure resulting from diverse etiologies. It is indicated for patients who show inadequate response to active medical treatment and/or artificial liver support therapy, or who fail to achieve improvement or recovery with these interventions. However, the widespread application of liver transplantation is significantly constrained by factors such as donor liver shortages, high procedural costs, technical complexity, and the risk of posttransplant rejection. Recent advances in ACLF treatment have introduced several promising approaches [Table ]. Cell-based therapies Mesenchymal

routinely recommended for ACLF outside of research trials. [ ] Liver transplantation is one of the most effective approaches for managing end-stage liver failure resulting from diverse etiologies. It is indicated for patients who show inadequate response to active medical treatment and/or artificial liver support therapy, or who fail to achieve improvement or recovery with these interventions. However, the widespread application of liver transplantation is significantly constrained by factors such as donor liver shortages, high procedural costs, technical complexity, and the risk of posttransplant rejection. Recent advances in ACLF treatment have introduced several promising approaches [Table ]. Cell-based therapies Mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) [ , ] and hepatocyte transplantation [ ] offer potential for liver regeneration and functional recovery, though large-scale clinical trials are needed to confirm their efficacy. Immunomodulation therapies Agents such as thymosin α1 [ ] and BTLA blockers [ ] aim to restore immune balance and enhance anti-infective capacity, addressing the immune dysregulation observed in ACLF. Cytokine-targeted therapies Drugs such as IL-22 promote liver regeneration [ , ] and have shown promise in early-phase clinical trials with good safety and a certain degree of efficiency (phase IIa in China, unpublished). Artificial liver support systems Nonbioartificial (e.g., double plasma molecular adsorption system [DPMAS] combined with plasma exchange [PE]) [ , ] or bioartificial liver systems, [ ] and novel devices like the DIALIVE liver dialysis system provide temporary support, bridging patients to recovery or liver transplantation. [ ] Gut–liver axis modulation Engineered carbon bead adsorbents reduce intestinal endotoxin levels, mitigating liver injury and SI. [ ] Pharmacological interventions Statins have shown potential in preventing the progression of cirrhosis to ACLF and reducing ACLF-related mortality, though further randomized controlled trials are needed. [ ] Despite these advancements, challenges remain, particularly in understanding the heterogeneous triggers of ACLF and standardizing treatment protocols. Future research should focus on large-scale, multicenter studies to validate these emerging therapies and refine therapeutic strategies. Conclusion and Prospect Although there is still no unified standard for the disease definition and diagnosis of ACLF worldwide, and there are still some differences in the descriptions of ACLF disease definitions by various associations or organizations around the world, with the gradual deepening of research, the clinical definition of the ACLF is more accurate and substantial progress is being made in the understanding of the pathogenesis of ACLF. ACLF has been widely recognized as a clinical syndrome different from ALF and CLF. Yet, only in recent years, key features of ACLF disease description, such as the basis of chronic liver diseases, acute intrahepatic or extrahepatic injury, acute hepatic decompensation, extrahepatic organ failure, high short-term mortality, and the reversibility of the disease course, have been systematically introduced, gradually narrowing the differences in disease definition between liver disease associations in the East and the West. However, there are still some differences in the evaluation standards for describing these key features, and it is urgent to carry out large-sample global multicenter prospective studies covering different etiologies and populations to achieve unification of the disease recognition and reach a consensus on ACLF definition in the East and the West. documents.title: AASLD Practice Guidance on Primary Biliary Cholangitis

chunks.content: The 2023 practice guidance on primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) and cholangiocarcinoma (CCA) of the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases (AASLD) came as a needful update to the previous 2010 guidelines on PSC, with a first-time inclusion of dedicated guidance on the diagnosis and management of CCA ( , ). This data-supported approach developed by consensus of an expert panel, provides guidance statements based on analytical review of the relevant literature. The production of guidance rather than guidelines relates to the paucity of sufficient randomized controlled trials suitable for systematic review and meta-analysis ( ). The publication is comprehensive, illustrative of remarkable progress since the 2010 guidelines, and will be a useful tool in providing high-quality care for these patient groups. Aside from the significant amount of new information and helpful recommendations, there is room to identify current gaps and future directions. The new terminology and clarifications about biliary strictures in PSC, including dominant, high-grade and relevant stricture, are valuable as they cover pre-existing gaps while promoting the use of a common language worldwide, as recently recommended by the International PSC Study Group ( , ). High-quality MRCP is recommended as the gold standard for diagnosis, while avoiding ERCP for diagnostic purposes is highlighted, owing to the increased risk of complications. The recently published guidelines of the European Association for the Study of the Liver (EASL) are less stringent on this matter but in agreement that MRCP is the preferred diagnostic tool ( ). While liver biopsy is fundamental to confirm a diagnosis of small-duct PSC or autoimmune hepatitis overlap ( ), it is not recommended for fibrosis staging in clinical practice ( , ). However, the role of liver histology in PSC has been recently revisited and is now considered essential in the regulatory approval process for new therapeutic strategies ( ). In the current landscape of intense development of surrogates of clinical endpoints, it is worth mentioning the recent data on collagen proportionate area (CPA), a quantitative method to measure the proportion of fibrosis on liver biopsy samples using digital image analysis. Further to the traditional histology scores, CPA provides useful information for risk-stratification and prognostication in PSC, and may be particularly useful in the clinical trials setting, for assessment of response-to-treatment and regression of fibrosis ( ). The utility of liver stiffness assessment by transient elastography or magnetic resonance elastography to estimate liver fibrosis and predict clinical outcomes, is increasingly recognised ( , ). Albeit not discussed in the new guidance, increasing evidence shows that the more recently developed elastographic techniques such as point- and 2D-/3D-shear wave elastography can be reliable for assessment of liver fibrosis and risk-stratification in PSC. Recent data on spleen stiffness as a predictor of presence of oesophageal varices in PSC are also encouraging ( ). Clinical prediction scores designed for PSC do not have generalised reliability and applicability; the 2023 practice guidance provides a useful diagram to guide the clinician in choosing, based on individual features ( ). Recommendations on the use of ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) in PSC have been inconsistent over time, and its potential to improve clinical outcomes remains unclear. However, a moderate dose of UDCA is now suggested as a possible treatment for patients not interested in or ineligible for clinical trials, since it may improve serum liver tests and surrogate markers of prognosis. The suggested dose, however, differs between the AASLD guidance (13–23 mg/kg/day) and the recent EASL guidelines (15–20 mg/kg/day) ( , ). As controversy still exists on the topic, further data is required to establish optimal doses. The 2023 AASLD guidance enumerates various pharmacological treatments currently investigated in clinical trials. It is worth also noting that faecal microbiota transplant has shown good safety profile and some preliminary efficacy signals in a recent pilot study, and is currently being further investigated ( ). The new guidance is the first ever to recommend the onset of colorectal cancer surveillance in patients with inflammatory bowel disease at the age of 15 years ( ). Notably, it recommends considering cholecystectomy for gallbladder polyps >8 mm, in contrast with the European guidelines from 2017, which suggested a cut-off size of >6 mm ( ), while the EASL guidelines recommend it for polyps ≥8 mm ( ). Furthermore, EASL suggests assessment of smaller polyps with contrast-enhanced ultrasound, and consideration of cholecystectomy if they enhance ( ). The new guidance appropriately differentiates de novo CCA and PSC-associated CCA, which owing to distinctive features should be seen indeed as different entities ( ). The provided diagnostic algorithm for relevant strictures in PSC is highly useful ( ). Some aspects are particularly interesting, including initial suspicious cytology warranting ERCP in 3 months, regardless of fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH) results ( ). It would be useful to assess the proportion of PSC patients

it for polyps ≥8 mm ( ). Furthermore, EASL suggests assessment of smaller polyps with contrast-enhanced ultrasound, and consideration of cholecystectomy if they enhance ( ). The new guidance appropriately differentiates de novo CCA and PSC-associated CCA, which owing to distinctive features should be seen indeed as different entities ( ). The provided diagnostic algorithm for relevant strictures in PSC is highly useful ( ). Some aspects are particularly interesting, including initial suspicious cytology warranting ERCP in 3 months, regardless of fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH) results ( ). It would be useful to assess the proportion of PSC patients ultimately diagnosed with CCA after recommended interval ERCP at 3 months and, subsequently, the proportion of those eligible for curative-intent treatment. Furthermore, clear recommendations are warranted for when initial negative/suspicious cytology with FISH polysomy is followed by ERCP revealing suspicious cytology with either FISH polysomy or negativity. Importantly, AASLD recommends that FISH should be obtained in all patients with suspected perihilar CCA (pCCA) or distal CCA (dCCA) ( ). While FISH has undoubtedly increased the diagnostic accuracy of biliary brushings cytology, it is not uniformly available for this purpose, including in prominent centres. It has to be underlined that the ongoing progress with liquid biopsies in different fronts, including diagnosis ( ), might result in the inclusion of this technique in future guidance and at various stages within the diagnostic algorithms. A few remarks on the valuable therapeutic algorithms for the three topographic categories of CCA can be drawn. A guidance statement explains that for unresectable liver-limited intrahepatic CCA (iCCA) orthotopic liver transplantation (OLT) should be considered under research protocols only ( ), while the schematic therapeutic algorithm recommends referral to a liver transplant centre for unresectable iCCA ≤2 cm. Although iCCA is still largely considered a contraindication for OLT, recent promising outcomes have led to the consensus statement recommendation by the European Network for the study of CCA that OLT should be considered as a potentially curative option especially in patients with very early stage unresectable iCCA (≤2 cm) and cirrhosis ( ). The guidance recommendation for resectable pCCA is “surgery followed by adjuvant chemotherapy”. Notably, in PSC-associated pCCA, surgical resection is most frequently precluded owing to various parameters including a higher rate of multifocal CCA, skip cancer lesions, poor quality of the liver parenchyma and hepatic dysfunction with reduced regenerative capacity ( , ). In contrast, the option of neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy followed by OLT is increasingly being recognised as the optimal treatment strategy and remains among the inclusion criteria of the Mayo Clinic protocol. The outcomes are superior compared to de novo pCCA ( , ), likely due to earlier detection in PSC owing to routine surveillance ( ) and a possible higher responsiveness to radiation therapy on a background of PSC ( , ). Extension into the distal bile duct is an established reason for consideration of combined OLT and pancreatoduodenectomy ( , ). The emphasis of the AASLD group on the Mayo Clinic protocolised approach to early pCCA is important, particularly as OLT for pCCA remains contraindicated in many countries despite the evidence of very good outcomes, on the background of the relative scarcity of donor organs. The TRANSPHIL trial ( NCT02232932 ), a French prospective open-label randomised multicentre comparative study ongoing since 2012, is aiming to clarify whether the best treatment for resectable pCCA is neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy followed by OLT or standard of care liver and bile duct resection. Should previous positive outcomes in favour of OLT be confirmed, this will lead to a true paradigm shift in the management of pCCA ( ). Notably, the trial lists PSC among the exclusion criteria for enrolment. Even without a statement regarding the role of lymphadenectomy, the practice guidance discusses that for iCCA in general, surgery involves liver resection and portal lymphadenectomy ( ). This approach is not uniformly accepted and the role of lymphadenectomy in this setting as a standard part of the surgical resection is under ongoing debate. Our recent meta-analysis showed that lymphadenectomy did not improve overall and disease-free survival, except in Japanese studies. However, lymph node metastases were found in 27.7% of patients undergoing lymphadenectomy, suggesting that it may aid in adequate staging ( ). Statements regarding the adequacy of lymphadenectomy in pCCA and dCCA are lacking. There is controversy on the matter in pCCA, with no established minimal number of harvested lymph nodes for histopathological assessment, while for dCCA, a minimum of 12 lymph nodes has been suggested as appropriate for accurate staging ( ). Firmer recommendations are anticipated in the future on this topic. When CCA extends both distally and towards the liver, attempts at hepatopancreatoduodenectomy have been challenging with high perioperative morbidity and mortality (97.4% and 26%, respectively, in recent series) and 5-year overall survival of 17.9–49.2% ( ). There is controversy on the matter in pCCA, with no established minimal number of harvested lymph nodes for histopathological assessment, while for dCCA, a minimum of 12 lymph nodes has been suggested as appropriate for accurate staging ( ). Firmer recommendations are anticipated in the future on this topic. When CCA extends both distally and towards the liver, attempts at hepatopancreatoduodenectomy have been challenging with high perioperative morbidity and mortality (97.4% and 26%, respectively, in recent series) and 5-year overall survival of 17.9–49.2% ( ). Accordingly, this procedure may be suitable to consider as a potentially curative approach only in very carefully selected fit patients. As underlined by the 2023 guidance, laparoscopic liver surgery is a safe approach for liver cancer ( ). Notably, the rapid accumulation of evidence with robotic surgery may soon define its place in the treatment of iCCA. In summary, the new AASLD practice guidance on PSC and CCA came at a suitable time and, compared with the guidelines from 2010, is highly indicative of the remarkable progresses made in understanding these diseases and their management. While it is expected to function as a valuable tool for specialists in the relevant fields, the current pace of progress is promising that further important outstanding questions may be answered in the near future.
