Definitions and grouping The diagnosis of ICP was established in pregnant women presenting with pruritus and raised serum TBA (fasting TBA ≥10 µmol/L or prandial TBA ≥19 µmol/L). Isolated ICP was defined as ICP occurring in the absence of viral hepatitis or other preexisting liver diseases. ICP involving CHB was defined as ICP complicated by CHB. Based on initial presentation of elevated TBA (for ICP involving CHB cases) or maternal liver dysfunction (for CHB with normal TBA cases), combined with the corresponding HBV DNA levels during pregnancy, the immune phases of CHB were categorized into 4 groups according to the definition of AASLD 2018 Hepatitis B Guidance: (1) immune-tolerant CHB: HBeAg-positive, serum HBV DNA >1×10 6 IU/mL, with normal or minimally elevated alanine transaminase (ALT) [<2× upper limit of normal (ULN)]; (2) inactive CHB: HBeAg-negative, anti-HBe–positive, HBV DNA <2×10 3 IU/mL, and normal ALT; (3) immune-active CHB: HBeAg-positive with HBV DNA >2×10 4 IU/mL, or HBeAg-negative with HBV DNA >2×10 3 IU/mL, and elevated ALT (≥2×ULN); (4) grey zone CHB: not meeting the criteria for any standard group. Data collection Clinical data and pregnancy outcomes for the enrolled pregnant women were extracted from electronic medical records. Maternal baseline information included age, educational level, parity, method of conception, previous history of ICP, pre-pregnancy body mass index (BMI), gestational weight gain, and gestational age at diagnosis of ICP. Key pregnancy outcomes encompassed obstetric complications, gestational age at delivery, mode of delivery, indications for iatrogenic preterm birth, fetal compromise, stillbirth, presence of MSAF, umbilical artery blood gas data, and neonatal outcomes. A composite adverse outcome was defined as any of the following: preterm birth, MSAF, Apgar scores 1 minute ≤7, umbilical artery pH <7.0, neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) admission, and stillbirth. Serial maternal biochemical liver function tests and hepatitis viral parameters were obtained from electronic laboratory systems, including TBA, ALT, aspartate aminotransferase (AST), albumin, total bilirubin (TB), direct bilirubin, albumin, gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase, alkaline phosphatase, cholinesterase, HBsAg, HBeAg, anti-HBe, HBV DNA levels. Statistical analysis Continuous variables were expressed as mean±standard deviation (SD), and differences between groups were assessed using one-way ANOVA. Categorical variables were reported as counts and percentages, and evaluated using chi-square tests or the Fisher exact test. Pairwise comparisons were performed with p -value adjusted by the Bonferroni correction for multiple testing. For pairwise comparisons between 2 subgroups, Student's t-test with Bonferroni correstion was chosen for homogeneous variances, while the Tamhane T2 test was utilized for heterogeneous variances. Multivariate analysis using a mixed-effects model was conducted to identify associated factors with adverse pregnancy outcomes. All statistical analyses were performed using the SPSS software (IBM, USA, version 27.0), and missing data were excluded from the statistical procedures. A 2-sided p -value <0.05 was considered statistically significant for all analyses. RESULTS Study population During the 13-year study period, a total of 83,426 pregnant women delivered their babies at the Third Affiliated Hospital of Sun Yat-sen University, and 1424 cases (1.7%) with elevated serum TBA were identified as a presumed ICP. According to the inclusion and exclusion criteria, the remaining 1172 pregnant women were enrolled and divided into 5 groups: isolated ICP group (n=826), ICP with immune-tolerant CHB (n=44), ICP with inactive CHB (n=86), ICP with immune-active CHB (n=127), and ICP with grey zone CHB (n=89). In addition, 87 cases of immune-active CHB with normal TBA levels were concurrently enrolled as a control cohort. The flowchart of the participant enrollment and grouping is shown in Figure . Clinical characteristics Baseline demographic and clinical data were summarized in Table . There were no significant differences among the 6 groups in terms of maternal age, parity, educational level, pre-pregnancy BMI, ICP in prior pregnancies, conception via assisted reproductive technology (ART), twin pregnancy, gestational diabetes mellitus, or hypertensive disorders of pregnancy ( p >0.05). Women in the immune-active CHB group had the least gestational weight gain compared with the other 5 groups ( p <0.05). Biochemical profiles of liver function This study collected maternal biochemical parameters of liver function among ICP groups at 4 pivotal time points: initial diagnosis of elevated TBA, peak TBA, the last recorded TBA within 1 week before delivery, and within 1 week after delivery. In the immune-active CHB with normal TBA group, data were collected at the following time points​​​​​​: initial presentation of abnormal liver function, peak ALT, the last recorded liver function within 1 week before delivery, and within 1 week after delivery. Results were presented in Figure and Supplemental Table S1, http://links.lww.com/HC9/C214 . Among ICP subgroups, the immune-tolerant, inactive, and grey zone CHB groups exhibited TBA levels comparable to those of the isolated ICP group throughout pregnancy, whereas the immune-active CHB group showed significantly higher TBA levels than the other 4 groups ( p <0.001). Despite some missing biochemical

week after delivery. In the immune-active CHB with normal TBA group, data were collected at the following time points​​​​​​: initial presentation of abnormal liver function, peak ALT, the last recorded liver function within 1 week before delivery, and within 1 week after delivery. Results were presented in Figure and Supplemental Table S1, http://links.lww.com/HC9/C214 . Among ICP subgroups, the immune-tolerant, inactive, and grey zone CHB groups exhibited TBA levels comparable to those of the isolated ICP group throughout pregnancy, whereas the immune-active CHB group showed significantly higher TBA levels than the other 4 groups ( p <0.001). Despite some missing biochemical data at various time points, ALT and AST levels exhibited slight fluctuations during pregnancy but maintained relatively consistent trends across the above 4 groups, except for 2 immune-active CHB groups. Notably, both immune-active CHB groups, with or without elevated TBA, showed relatively higher ALT and AST levels during pregnancy, followed by a notable decrease before delivery. Meanwhile, TB levels remained stable throughout pregnancy in all 6 groups. After delivery, patients with normal liver function rarely underwent repeat laboratory testing, and postpartum biochemical data were predominantly available for women exhibiting pre-delivery biochemical abnormalities. In the isolated ICP group and immune-tolerant, inactive, and grey zone CHB subgroups, postpartum average levels of ALT, AST, and TB showed slight elevations compared with pre-delivery values. Conversely, in cases of ICP with immune-active CHB, where most patients already had abnormal liver function before delivery, the average levels of ALT and AST notably decreased after delivery. However, the average TBA concentrations rapidly returned to near-normal ranges within 1 week after delivery in all subgroups. Detailed characteristics of other serum biochemical profiles for isolated ICP, ICP with CHB subgroups, and immune-active CHB with the normal TBA group were summarized in Supplemental Table S1, http://links.lww.com/HC9/C214 . Stratification of TBA levels revealed that the ICP with immune-active CHB group exhibited the highest frequency of TBA levels ≥100 µmol/L throughout pregnancy compared with the other 4 groups ( p <0.001, Supplemental Table S1 http://links.lww.com/HC9/C214 , and Supplemental Figure S1, http://links.lww.com/HC9/C213 ), with 39.4% (50/127) at peak levels and 24.4% (31/127) at last recorded measurement, respectively. Within 1 week postpartum, nearly 80% of these women were retested for TBA, with 52.0% (53/102) continuing elevated TBA levels >10 µmol/L, 10.8% (11/102) having TBA levels of 40–99.9 µmol/L, and 6.9% (7/102) having levels ≥100 µmol/L (Supplemental Table S1, http://links.lww.com/HC9/C214 ). HBV parameters Consistent with the diagnostic criteria, the immune-tolerant CHB group displayed the significantly highest rates of HBeAg positivity and elevated initial HBV DNA levels among all 5 groups ( p <0.001). Consequently, a majority (70.4%) received antiviral therapy, predominantly (93.5%) for prevention of mother-to-child transmission before ICP diagnosis. While in the ICP with immune-active CHB group, 87.5% of antiviral therapies were indicated for the management of active hepatitis, either before or after ICP diagnosis. When compared with the cases of ICP with immune-active CHB, patients with immune-active CHB and normal TBA exhibited a higher rate of HBeAg positivity, elevated initial HBV DNA levels, and an increased rate of antiviral therapy (Table ). Pregnancy outcomes Despite the comparable gestational age at initial diagnosis of elevated TBA to the other 4 subgroups, the ICP with immune-active CHB group reached peak TBA levels significantly earlier ( p <0.001), taking ~2 weeks compared with 4–6 weeks for others. For gestational age at delivery, pregnant women in this group experienced the earliest deliveries and the highest risk of total preterm birth, particularly notable for early preterm births occurring <32 weeks and <34 weeks ( p <0.001). Moreover, these women also had the highest proportions of iatrogenic preterm birth due to elevated TBA levels, deliveries via cesarean section, and presence of MSAF, and subsequently with the lowest neonatal birthweight, highest frequencies of NICU admission ( p <0.05). In contrast, pregnancy outcomes in the ICP with other CHB subgroups were similar to those of isolated ICP cases. DISCUSSION This large retrospective cohort study elucidated the longitudinal liver biochemical profiles and pregnancy outcomes of women diagnosed with ICP, with or without CHB, and simultaneously analyzed the differences in these parameters based on the stage of CHB. We observed that patients with ICP involving immune-tolerant, inactive, and grey zone CHB had similar biochemical patterns and outcomes with isolated ICP cases. Women with ICP involving immune-active CHB experienced the most severe biochemical abnormalities and adverse outcomes. Conversely, despite showing relatively higher initial transaminase levels, women with immune-active CHB with normal TBA exhibited the best obstetric and neonatal outcomes among all groups. Multivariable analysis found that assisted reproductive technology, peak TBA levels ≥40 µmol/L, and ICP involving immune-active CHB were associated with increased risk of composite adverse outcomes. Moreover, after adjusting for potential confounders, stratified analysis revealed that peak TBA levels of 40–99.9 µmol/L and ≥100 µmol/L significantly increased the risks of preterm birth, iatrogenic preterm birth, and NICU admission; while TBA levels ≥100 µmol/L were additionally associated with elevated risk of MSAF and Apgar scores 1 minute ≤7. Three out of 4 stillbirths recorded in this cohort occurred between 27 and 33 gestational weeks, with peak TBA levels ≥100 µmol/L. As a multifactorial and pregnancy-specific hepatic disorder, the etiology of ICP is complex. Accumulated data have demonstrated that HBV infection is a well-documented risk factor for developing ICP. However, both ICP and CHB can present with elevated liver enzymes and TBA levels, complicating their differentiation. Consequently, some studies, systematic reviews, and academic guidelines have approached ICP as a diagnosis of exclusion, specifically excluding patients with CHB. This diagnostic strategy may create a knowledge gap regarding the interaction between ICP and CHB, as well as their potential synergistic impacts on pregnancy outcomes. Furthermore, the absence of robust evidence may also compromise clinical management of pregnant women experiencing ICP coexisting with different phases of CHB. Our findings showed that women with ICP concurrent immune-active CHB exhibited the highest levels of TBA, ALT, AST, and TB throughout pregnancy compared with other subgroups. This biochemical profile underscores the severe hepatic burden from immune-active CHB. However, patients with ICP involving other stages of CHB displayed biochemical profiles similar

This biochemical profile underscores the severe hepatic burden from immune-active CHB. However, patients with ICP involving other stages of CHB displayed biochemical profiles similar to isolated ICP cases from initial diagnosis to post-delivery, reflecting the transient nature of ICP-related biochemical changes without pronounced active hepatitis. Therefore, in CHB patients who have not progressed to the immune-active phase, the presence of elevated TBA, with or without mild ALT flares, should prompt clinical consideration for ICP rather than solely attributing it to CHB. Conversely, the sustained ALT elevation in the immune-active CHB group suggests a more prominent chronic hepatic inflammation beyond ICP-associated liver dysfunction. Collectively, these findings highlight the crucial role of liver biochemical markers and HBV serology in determining the underlying etiology of liver dysfunction in pregnant women. In addition, this study reaffirms that CHB should not be routinely excluded as a risk factor in the diagnostic workup of ICP. Numerous studies have established that maternal TBA levels are pivotal in determining the risk of adverse pregnancy outcomes associated with ICP. Consistent with previous observation, our multivariable analysis further revealed a positive association between peak TBA levels and the risk of adverse outcomes, including total and iatrogenic preterm birth, MSAF, low Apgar score, NICU admission, and composite adverse outcomes, regardless of the presence or absence of CHB. However, despite exhibiting relatively higher transaminase levels at the initial diagnosis, immune-active CHB women with normal TBA achieved more favorable pregnancy outcomes than other CHB subgroups with elevated TBA levels. These findings indicated that the association between TBA levels and ICP-related adverse outcomes could also be applicable to cases involving CHB, thereby reinforcing the significance of bile acids as a critical biomarker for risk stratification in ICP involving CHB. Furthermore, women with ICP concurrent immune-active CHB not only displayed the highest TBA levels but also experienced the most composite adverse outcomes. This observation could be explained by 2 potential mechanisms: ​​​​​a potential synergistic effect of immune-active CHB on hepatic injury and pregnancy outcomes in the context of elevated TBA levels, or a dominant role of uncontrolled hepatitis activity rather than ICP itself. Antiviral therapy can effectively suppress viral replication, prevent mother-to-child transmission, and improve liver function, making it a crucial component in the management of CHB during pregnancy. In this study, we further examined its effect on pregnancy outcomes in cases of immune-active CHB with ICP. Stratified analysis found that antiviral treatment significantly reduced the rates of iatrogenic preterm birth and cesarean section. These findings suggest that antiviral intervention may mitigate liver dysfunction and improve adverse pregnancy outcomes in the setting of CHB with elevated TBA levels. However, interpretation of these results is limited by the lack of detailed data on medication adherence and maternal acceptance. As a rare but catastrophic event, ICP-related stillbirth typically occurs suddenly without warning precursors, with reported rates ranging from 0.15% to 1.5%. A comprehensive meta-analysis involving 5269 ICP cases demonstrated a significantly increased risk of stillbirth only when TBA levels reached 100 µmol/L (3.4% when TBA≥100 µmol/L vs. 0.3% when TBA of 10-40 µmol/L), particularly after 35 gestational weeks. Subsequently, several international guidelines recommended planned delivery at 35–36 weeks for women with peak TBA levels ≥100 µmol/L. It is noteworthy that the Chinese guideline for ICP was updated in 2024, while our study cohort was managed following earlier guidelines (issued in 2011 and 2015), which recommended delivery beyond 34 weeks and 36 weeks when TBA exceeded 40 µmol/L, respectively. This historical context likely contributed to our higher frequency of iatrogenic preterm births before TBA levels reached 100 µmol/L, potentially explaining the observed low stillbirth rate of 0.2% at TBA levels of 40–99.9 µmol/L and 2.4% at TBA levels ≥100 µmol/L. Recent national data from the United States (2015–2020) reported that earlier deliveries in ICP patients resulted in lower stillbirth rates compared with non-ICP controls, underscoring the effectiveness of contemporary strategies to reduce stillbirth risk at the expense of increased preterm births. However, in our cohort, 3 stillbirths occurred between 27 and 33 weeks of gestation with peak TBA levels >100 µmol/L, much earlier than current guidelines recommendations. This highlights the ongoing clinical challenge in managing ICP with high TBA levels, as clinicians must continually balance the competing risks of iatrogenic preterm delivery and stillbirth. A notable and unexpected finding was the increased occurrence of MSAF in the ICP with immune-active CHB group, with rates of 26.9% (14/52) at peak TBA levels of 40–99.9 µmol/L and 50.0% (25/50) at peak TBA levels ≥100 µmol/L. These rates were much higher than those observed in our isolated ICP cases and previous reports. In addition, the incidence of MSAF in the immune-active CHB with normal TBA group was 12.6% (11/87), comparable to the isolated ICP group. Nevertheless, it remains unclear whether the chronic liver inflammation induced by immune-active CHB is responsible for these elevated MSAF rates. Larger case–control cohort studies including more pregnant women who suffered CHB, with or without raised TBA levels, are needed to further evaluate the impact of CHB on MSAF risk. The primary strength of our study lies in the first attempt to comprehensively analyze the longitudinal biochemical profiles and pregnancy outcomes in a large cohort of women with isolated ICP and ICP involving various phases of CHB. Furthermore, the stratified analysis by TBA levels and CHB immune status provides nuanced insights into the correlation between bile acids and adverse pregnancy outcomes, as well as the underlying diagnostic approaches for ICP in the context of CHB. Even with limited postpartum laboratory data available, observed changes in biochemical parameters can offer valuable insights into different phases of CHB during pregnancy. However, there are several limitations that merit consideration. First, the retrospective design precluded the standardization of laboratory investigations for ICP and CHB cases, leading to incomplete data for certain biochemical markers at some time points, which would introduce bias in the analysis of longitudinal biochemical profiles. Secondly, the retrospective extraction of ICP diagnosis from inpatient electronic medical records may have led to potential diagnostic misclassification of ICP, particularly among women with immune-active CHB experiencing ALT flares. Thirdly, ICP cases were managed according to China’s guidelines over a 13-year period, potentially limiting the generalizability of our findings. Nonetheless, our comprehensive dataset provides important real-world evidence for evaluating the impact of these ICP management practices on pregnancy outcomes within China over the past decade. In addition, the assignment of CHB phases was based on laboratory parameters from a single time point at the initial diagnosis, potentially not capturing the dynamics of CHB immune status during pregnancy. Lastly, the absence of detailed treatment information, including the dosing, duration, and adherence to ursodeoxycholic acid and antiviral agents, hinders drawing conclusions regarding specific management strategies. CONCLUSIONS Pregnant women with ICP involving immune-active CHB experienced the most severe biochemical abnormalities and adverse pregnancy outcomes, likely due to the compounded influence of both CHB and elevated TBA levels. Whereas, ICP with other stages of CHB (immune-tolerant, inactive, or grey zone) exhibited biochemical patterns and outcome risks comparable to isolated ICP, indicating that elevated TBA levels, with or without mild ALT flares, are primarily driven by transient changes associated with ICP rather than CHB. Multivariable analysis identified peak TBA levels as a critical biomarker for evaluating the risk of adverse pregnancy outcomes in all ICP cases, irrespective of coexisting CHB. Overall, this study highlights the clinical importance of tailoring diagnostic approaches, surveillance protocols, and management strategies according to TBA levels and the immune phase of CHB.
